BreakingNewsTab.title: Barristers must stop using rape myths in trials, justice secretary says
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The justice secretary has called for new rules to prevent barristers from using rape myths to defend their clients in the wake of the Russell Brand trial.

As first reported by the Times, external, in a letter to the Bar Standards Board (BSB), Alex Norris said it was "unacceptable" to "perpetuate myths" about victims in court and disciplinary action could be taken against those who do so.

In his closing speech, Brand's defence barrister, Ian Winter KC, questioned why his client's accusers had not fought back.

The BSB said it had set up an expert group this year to advise on "strengthening standards for barristers", while the Bar Council said defendants had a "right to have evidence tested in court".

Brand was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

Winter said to the court "not one of them [Brand's accusers] resisted or screamed or even tried to leave".

Winter also asked the jury if they could be sure that out of the "many, many women" Brand had had sex with over a decade, "he raped just three of them".

Norris wrote in his letter to the BSB: "[The board] must send a strong signal to the profession on the harm arising from rape myths, and that the perpetuation of such myths within a court room is unacceptable, just as they are unacceptable in our society at large."

The charity Rape Crisis says it is "really common for people who experience rape, sexual assault, sexual abuse or other types of sexual violence to find they can't move or speak".

The judge presiding over Brand's case was praised by the Criminal Bar Association and campaign groups for comments he made during his sentencing remarks to dispel rape myths.

Mr Justice Bennathan told Southwark Crown Court: "Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no and to demand justice from the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Russell Brand, act without their consent."

A spokesperson for the BSB said such cases "must be decided on the basis of the evidence and not prejudice", adding: "Any other approach may discourage others from coming forward and adversely affect public confidence in the criminal justice system more widely."

Kirsty Brimelow KC, chair of the Bar Council of England and Wales which is part of the group examining the need for further training, said it was important for the BSB to remain "independent of the government".

She told BBC Radio 4's Woman's Hour that a "regulatory gap" had not been made clear to her and there were already powers to discipline barristers if breaches of the code of conduct happen.

She said training for "vulnerable witnesses" was already undertaken but it could be "problematic" if it was made mandatory.

Brimelow said there were currently a lack of barristers defending cases of rape and sexual assault and the possibility of further compulsory training could see more pushed out.

"What I wouldn't like to see is publicity around one case to take a life of its own rather than looking at what we already do," she told the BBC.

A spokesperson for the Ministry of Justice said the justice secretary was "determined to make protections for victims as strong as possible".

"Rape myths have absolutely no place in our courts, giving evidence in cases of this nature is a brave act and can be traumatic for victims: they must never feel as though they are the ones on trial," the spokesperson said.

"Independent judges are already able to, and do, give directions to counter rape myths but we always want to keep looking at ways we can improve how the entire justice system treats victims of sexual violence."

BreakingNewsTab.title: Yemeni forces retreat to defend Aden from Houthis
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia say they are redeploying troops to defend the country's interim capital, Aden, following weeks of intensified fighting with the Iran-backed Houthi movement.

The Southern Armed Forces said it was withdrawing from an area overlooking the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, at the southern end of the Red Sea, to reinforce positions around Aden and neighbouring areas.

Houthi-run media say the movement has taken control of the evacuated territory. Saudi Arabia has not commented.

The shift ends a weeks-long offensive to try to secure the area near the key shipping route which the Houthis seized in a surprise offensive in September.

Pro-government forces said they had "secured" the strait in early October as they sought to retake crucial ground from the Houthis. The Iran-backed fighters said they had captured areas including Perim Island at the mouth of the strait and the strategic port city of Mokha a month prior.

But the Saudi-backed Southern Armed Forces fighting on behalf of Yemen's internationally recognised government said on Sunday they were withdrawing to reinforce troops elsewhere, with the southern city of Aden a "priority".

It said troops were being withdrawn "from Dhubab Airport and the Bab al-Mandab area" with the aim of "strengthening the front lines and addressing existing threats".

"This step is driven by the priority of securing the capital, Aden, and neighbouring governorates, reinforcing the front lines and addressing existing threats."

The Houthis said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway when they captured territory overlooking it, but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.

However, the seizure contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz.

A UN Human Rights spokesperson, Ravina Shamdasani, urged all parties to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure.

She noted that since the escalation of fighting in August, more than 60% of documented civilian casualties were women and children.

The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Aden in recent weeks, including an assault on 15 October that targeted the presidential palace, killing five and injuring 16.

Saudi Arabia responded with hundreds of air strikes, while the Houthis launched hundreds of drones and missiles at its cities and infrastructure.

The UN has estimated that nearly 330,000 people have been displaced in Yemen as the fighting has since escalated. Hundreds of people are reported to have been killed.

BreakingNewsTab.title: South Africa shootings: 17 killed in Pietermaritzburg and Pretoria
BreakingNewsTab.text:
South African police are investigating the murders of 17 people in two separate shootings on Sunday night.

Eight men were fatally shot in a minibus in KwaZulu-Natal province. Police declared them dead when they arrived at the scene. Hours later, nine people were found shot dead inside a shack in western Pretoria.

Police say the two incidents are unrelated. The motive for the shootings has not yet been established.

South Africa is struggling to contain violent crime, including gang-related killings. The country has one of the world's highest murder rates.

Police say they responded to reports of a shooting ⁠outside Pietermaritzburg town in KwaZulu-Natal and found a white seven-seater vehicle riddled with bullet holes.

Inside were eight men with multiple gunshot wounds.

"It has not been established how the incident happened, and police are collecting pieces of evidence to determine the possible motive of the killings and the identity of the suspects," police spokesperson Robert Netshiunda said.

The police have launched a manhunt for the suspects.

In a separate shooting in the Jeffsville informal settlement in Atteridgeville, west of Pretoria, police found the bodies of six men and three women.

They are believed to have been killed inside a four-room shack between 22:00 and 23:00 on Sunday. The bodies were scattered across the rooms, with several spent cartridges discovered outside the shack.

Community members initially mistook the gunshots for thunder and lightning.

"The provincial commissioner of police in Gauteng [province, which includes Pretoria] has mobilized the necessary resources, including the crime intelligence and the deputy provincial commissioner tracking team to search for the suspect," police spokesperson Brigadier Brenda Muridili said.

It's not the first mass shooting in the area. In January, five men were shot dead outside a local shop in broad daylight.

Illegal firearms are widespread in South Africa, where gun violence remains a persistent problem, increasingly involving mass shootings.

In September, 28 people were killed in two separate cases.

Eighteen people were killed when eight gunmen stormed a bar near Johannesburg and opened fire on 25 September. Fourteen others were injured.

In a separate shooting the following day, 10 people were killed outside an entertainment venue in a township near Cape Town. A further 11 were injured.

Much of the violence has been linked to turf wars between gangs involved in drug trafficking and illegal mining.

In February, President Cyril Ramaphosa described organised crime as "the most immediate threat to our democracy, our society and our economic development".

Earlier this year, the military was deployed alongside police to five provinces with the highest murder rates, including Gauteng, in an effort to tackle armed violence.

According to the latest police statistics, 5,427 people were murdered nationwide between April and June 2026, an average of about 60 killings a day. This was a 6% decline compared with the same period a year earlier.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Ashes of exiled Nobel Laureate Miguel Ángel Asturias returned to Guatemala
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The remains of writer and diplomat Miguel Ángel Asturias have been buried in his native Guatemala 52 years after he died in exile.

His ashes were brought to Guatemala from Paris, where he had lived before his death from cancer in the Spanish capital, Madrid, in 1974.

Asturias was awarded the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1967 for his vivid writings, which drew on the experiences of indigenous Guatemalans.

The urn containing his ashes was placed in soil gathered from different parts of Guatemala at a cultural centre named after him in Guatemala City.

His son, whose name is also Miguel Ángel Asturias, said at the ceremony on Sunday: "I can tell you, old man, that you are with us, you are in your homeland, you will sleep beneath your own skies."

Asturias, who was born in 1899, first moved to Paris in the 1920s to study ethnology.

Influenced by the surrealists, he wrote his first major work, Legends of Guatemala, a retelling of Maya origin legends and mythological tales, while in France.

Subsequent works, such as the 1946 novel The President and his Banana Trilogy, denounced the terrors of dictatorship in Latin America and the exploitation indigenous workers suffered on banana plantations.

Arguably his most famous novel was Men of Maize, published in 1949, which explores the struggles of indigenous communities as the world around them quickly changes and modernises.

FinanceTab.title: Faisal Islam: What's in the Brexit reset food deal and are there trade-offs?
FinanceTab.text:
In Boston, Lincolnshire, a supplier of ready meals to Marks & Spencer (M&S) manufactures thousands of portions of spaghetti bolognese to be sent to the retailer's shops in the Republic of Ireland.

Every plastic pallet is meticulously individually tagged with a green-grey label “Eire”.

It has been this way since Brexit.

Every truck full of food sent to European Union countries requires hundreds of pages of forms, checks by vets, expense and delays.

It has cost M&S millions of pounds and is part of that reason the British business shut down 11 French stores in 2021.

Many smaller exporters stopped sending their goods to the EU entirely. Some produce, including sausages and certain types of seafood, were entirely stopped.

All this was the predictable consequence of former Prime Minister Boris Johnson’s 2020 deal prioritising regulatory freedom over freeflowing goods trade.

That will end with a Brexit "reset" that Prime Minister Andy Burnham is set to sign with the EU on Friday.

The government claims it could boost the economy to the tune of £5bn a year and cut the cost of food for households.

But will the agreement mean a return to frictionless trade for food with the EU or are there trade-offs and quid pro quos the UK will have to make?

EU affairs minister Hamish Falconer, who is a key negotiator with the bloc, acknowledged a “choice” is being made.

In exchange for being able to export produce such as Lincolnshire sausages to the 27 countries, the flipside is the extent to which the UK will be able to influence EU food policies.

The UK will have a "voice in the room", said Falconer, but no vote. Critics have said a reset will make the UK "a rule taker", not a rule maker.

But Falconer said the UK will be involved in a process to shape the rules.

A Brexit reset would not involve any upfront payments, said Falconer, but made it clear there could well be an "exit clause" in case a future UK government reversed the closer alignment.

He said this was "reasonable" to consider what would happen if a future Conservative or Reform government wanted to undo the new arrangements. Both parties have said they would if they were in power.

"The EU is worried about that and you can see why," he said.

The BBC understands that the clause is a result of EU concerns about the possible cost of having to rebuild facilities for border food safety checks which were put in place following Brexit.

The reset means they will be dismantled.

The prime minister has said he believes there is a "win-win" deal to be had with the EU.

Speaking at a Marks & Spencer food court in central London, Falconer said reducing the cost of importing food "will mean less cost for supermarkets, and I hope that less cost then turns into cheaper produce on the shelves".

He said companies have to currently deal with "pages and pages" of form-filling.

Some exports are rejected for having the wrong colour of ink on forms, or an inaccurate Latin name for cooked meats.

The reset could also mean "tearing up" checks that were introduced on goods flowing from Great Britain to Northern Ireland, following Brexit, he said, as well as separate "Not for EU" labelling.

The whole deal to be signed on Friday is calculated to add 0.4% to UK GDP.

Another contentious area has been crisp flavourings, with concerns raised that stricter EU rules on certain ingredients might limit the sale of some popular snack flavours in the UK.

"I want to take this opportunity to absolutely stamp down on misinformation about smoky bacon crisps," Falconer said.

Post-Brexit the UK had stayed "pretty closely aligned" to European food safety standards, he said.

Two leading snack brands had already adapted their recipes to accommodate EU rules, an example of the kind of alignment that would happen whether or not there was a reset of UK-EU relations.

"The truth is, almost every business in this country that wants to export food or drink will be aligning with EU rules because it's our biggest market.

"Lots of people, like the good people at Walkers and Frazzles have made these changes already, so I would want to reassure people, particularly smoky bacon fans, it's okay," he said.

FinanceTab.title: Intel sued by investors after PC sales slump hits share price
FinanceTab.text:
Intel, the US chip giant, is being sued by its shareholders who accuse the firm of hiding the severity of a slump in its personal computer (PC) sales that caused its share price to plunge almost 29% in one day.

Billions of dollars was knocked off the value of the company after it forecast disappointing revenues ahead of its latest earnings report.

Shareholders allege that Intel made "materially false and misleading" statements that failed to disclose the slowdown in PC sales and the impact of its data centre projects, according to a proposed class action lawsuit filed in San Jose, California.

The BBC has contacted Intel for comment.

In October, Intel firm announced its computer hardware sales had dropped sharply in the three months that ended in September.

That report undermined earlier suggestions from the chipmaker that demand had been improving, sending Intel shares plunging, according to the lawsuit.

Shareholders claimed the "depressed demand for PC sales" caused "a dramatic slowdown" in quarterly earnings – a drop of 9%, or about $800m - to $8.1bn.

The lawsuit, filed by legal firm Robbins Geller Rudman & Dowd on behalf of owners of Intel common shares between 23 July and 29 October this year, was filed against the chipmaker, its chief executive Tan Lip-Bu and other company leaders.

Intel has poured huge investments into manufacturing to meet the enormous demand for AI computing power.

As more semiconductors are channelled towards data centres, chips for PCs and other electronics have become more expensive.

Intel boss Tan had told analysts that the industry was facing an "unprecedented memory crunch", resulting in a shortage of chip supplies for PCs.

"We need to address these challenges with urgency," Tan said in October.

Intel shares have fallen sharply in the past month by 37.5%, though its share price is still up by 51% overall this year.

FinanceTab.title: Gas starts flowing from Jackdaw after government green light
FinanceTab.text:
Gas has begun flowing from the Jackdaw gas field, with the UK energy secretary saying it will help to heat millions of homes and businesses this winter.

Ministers last month announced the Jackdaw field, which lies 150 miles east of Aberdeen, had been approved after years of uncertainty and a court case.

It has now been announced that it has begun producing gas which will start flowing into Britain, according to its operator Adura.

The UK government approved production from the gas field in the North Sea last month, amid intense debate about the project's environmental and economic impact.

Jackdaw is operated by Adura under a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor.

A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said: "Last month, I gave Jackdaw the green light and today its gas will start flowing into Britain, thanks to the hard work of the skilled North Sea workers.

"It means homegrown gas from this project will help to heat millions of British homes and businesses this winter and beyond, in a boost for our energy security.

"It also will help minimise the UK's use of imported higher emission gas as we continue our transition to renewables and nuclear."

Claire Mueller, Jackdaw project director at Adura, said the gas field was "now helping to power Britain".

She added: "At a time of considerable uncertainty around the world, Jackdaw will provide secure energy from our own waters to heat British homes and power our economy, while reducing our reliance on imports with higher emissions.

"Jackdaw also demonstrates what can be achieved when Britain makes pragmatic, evidence-led decisions about the energy it needs, while properly accounting for our climate responsibilities."

Mueller said the decision was a "positive step towards restoring confidence in the North Sea".

She added that Adura was "proud to be producing the oil and gas our country will continue to need for decades".

Adura has said Jackdaw will provide about 6% of UK gas production, enough to power 1.4 million homes. After imports are included, that amounts to about 2% of total UK demand.

The gas will be pumped to the existing Shearwater platform for processing – known as a tie-back in industry terms – before being piped to the St Fergus gas terminal in Aberdeenshire.

The UK government said that over its expected 11-year lifespan, Jackdaw would support the UK's gas supply, protect hundreds of jobs and add £2.9bn to the economy.

The decision to green-light Jackdaw drew criticism from some Labour backbenchers and environmentalists, while Conservatives called on the government to also approve the Rosebank oil field.

Both projects were approved for development by the previous Tory government in 2022 and 2023 respectively but these decisions were struck down by the Scottish courts after a challenge from environmental campaigners.

This followed a Supreme Court ruling that developers had to account for the climate impact caused by burning fossil fuels in their planning applications.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to stick to the UK's net zero target despite giving the green light to Jackdaw.

He previously said the decision would "significantly strengthen our energy security by increasing domestic gas production by about 6% and support the UK's energy supply for more than a decade".

A decision on the larger Rosebank oil project is yet to be made.

The co-leader of the Scottish Greens, Ross Greer, described the Jackdaw approval as "climate vandalism".

He said: "It is a devastating betrayal of our children's future and it won't even lower energy bills in the here and now."

Environmental campaigners argue that this summer's heatwaves demonstrate the need to tackle climate change by rejecting both Jackdaw and Rosebank.

Areeba Hamid, the co-executive director of Greenpeace, said approving Jackdaw was "the wrong decision" in terms of lowering energy bills, providing energy security, and addressing climate change.

Oxfam said the government had "drilled straight through the UK's climate commitments" and accused the prime minister of sending "the wrong signal as the impacts of climate change intensify".

The charity says the government must commit to not approving any new oil and gas licences, including the proposals for Rosebank.

When BBC News visited the platform this summer, Adura CEO Neil McCulloch said its approval was vital to avoid domestic supply shortages this winter.

However, the UK government has previously suggested that Jackdaw will have little impact on energy security and none on reducing domestic gas and electricity bills.

In August, in an interim response to a consultation on the future of the country's gas supplies, Energy Minister Michael Shanks said the UK would inevitably become more reliant on imports as domestic production declined, external.

"With diminishing output from the North Sea over the past decades, any gas produced from the UK Continental Shelf represents a tiny fraction of global demand and so will not lower prices nor materially boost supply," wrote Shanks.

Labour has previously said it is opposed to the issuing of new exploration licences but it will consider new production projects if they are tied back to existing facilities.

McCulloch described the Jackdaw decision as "an important and positive step forward" - but said attention now turned to Rosebank.

He has urged the UK government to approve production from the field, in which Adura owns an 80% stake. The other 20% is held by London-based Ithaca Energy.

Rosebank contains an estimated 300 million to 500 million barrels of oil.

But while most of Jackdaw's gas is likely to be consumed in the UK, Rosebank's oil will be taken off by tanker and sold on international markets.

FinanceTab.title: Avoid this Black Friday scam - how to check it's a real deal
FinanceTab.text:
This month's Black Friday and the tax return deadline at the end of January are both opportunities for fraudsters to scam you.

That's because people are more likely to expect emails, texts and other correspondence at this time of year.

Fraudsters will use the dates to impersonate genuine organisations and retailers by pushing victims towards fake websites to steal personal information.

Here's how to spot a scam and how you can avoid being caught out.

If you are self-employed or have more than one source of income you will need to file a tax return by the end of January.

Fraudsters seize on this deadline to blitz people with messages that look like they are official and from the UK's tax authority, HMRC.

Any such calls or messages should be ignored, but you can also check whether an email, external, text message, external or phone call, external claiming to be from HMRC is genuine.

"Reporting scams helps us shut them down and protect others," adds Lucy Pike, HMRC's chief security officer.

New figures from HMRC, shared with the BBC, show that it received 95,340 reports of suspected scams in the year to the end of October.

There were 900 reports of one specific scam which used emails containing a malicious attachment which directed customers to a fake gov.uk webpage designed to steal personal and financial information.

To avoid being caught out, HMRC says:

it never contacts people by email, text or phone to tell them they are due a refund or ask them to claim one

it never asks for personal or financial information by email or text message

it never leaves threatening voicemails about legal action or arrest

FinanceTab.title: Beauty advent calendars can cost hundreds - but are they value for money?
FinanceTab.text:
It's easy to see the appeal of a beauty advent calendar. Like many women at this time of year, Julia says she often finds herself tempted to splurge on one - especially a perfume calendar. But she takes quite an unsentimental approach.

"I always look at what's in them. If I like enough of the fragrances, I'll buy it," says the 39-year old, who works as a senior commercial manager in engineering.

Luxury advent calendars are supposed to offer the thrill of a surprise but, for Julia, it is more important she actually wants the items inside - a thought that is also striking more and more customers in the wake of the scandal over the Skims calendar.

This week, Kim Kardashian's beauty brand offered all of its customers refunds for its $148 (£110) calendar after being widely criticised on social media over the quality of its contents, with some customers likening the hair clips, scrunchies and keychains inside to things you might find down the back of a sofa.

Julia says she earns a good salary but is keen to get value for money and doesn't want to waste it on items she won't use.

"I spent £160 on a Space NK fragrance calendar last year," she says. "I got some fragrances I'd been wanting for a while for a lot less than recommended retail price, and those I didn't like I managed to sell on for a slight mark-up on what I paid."

Beauty calendars, which often cost upwards of £100 and sometimes much more, have been around for more than a decade and the marketing has grown ever more sophisticated.

High-profile brands will warn that their calendars risk running out, which may boost early demand, while unboxing videos posted by influencers can encourage spending by creating an infectious sense of surprise and delight.

And it appears to be working. Ipsos data shows, external around 15% of all advent calendars sold are beauty ones, with people aged 18-34 particularly willing to splash out.

But in the face of that tsunami of marketing, customers seem to be getting savvier.

"I love beauty, but I rarely buy beauty advent calendars. They are pricey and often only have a few things that I actually want to try or are trending products," says Priya Raj, 30, a fashion journalist.

She thinks some are good value but, for her, the advantage is being able to try on a small scale without forking out for a full-size product.

"For me, an advent calendar - particularly a beauty one - serves the purpose of allowing me to try out different products, particularly in the lead-up to Christmas, and then I can hopefully snag a bargain in the Boxing Day sales."

Podcaster Rhea Somaiya, 28, also likes the general idea, but has a healthy scepticism around a lot of them in practice.

"I do think some brands take the consumer for granted in that they provide each day with something so menial that people are bombarded with irrelevant and cluttering items.

"And when that's the case, they certainly put me off as the excitement to open each window dwindles into irritation rather than joy."

Heather Widdows, a beauty expert and philosophy professor at Warwick University, has pointed out that while you might buy some of the products in an advent calendar individually, it's highly unlikely you'd buy all of them.

"Beauty calendars may offer you lots of products for a really good price. They can also be a bit of fun and feel sensuous.

"But it is exceptionally unlikely that you would use all the products inside them, so they're probably not worth it."

This year, Julia has spent £99 on a John Lewis fragrance calendar which she thinks is good value for money. But it doesn't mean she'll keep everything in it.

In fact she's joined a Facebook group where people trade the ones they don't want for ones they do.

"The ones I keep are already a lot cheaper per mililitre than if you bought them at retail," she says.

With additional reporting from Kris Bramwell

FinanceTab.title: Pat McFadden backs legal right to job support for young people
FinanceTab.text:
The work and pensions secretary has backed the idea that the government should legally guarantee young people help to get into employment.

Pat McFadden told the BBC that job support should be given a "legislative underpinning", adding the level of assistance on offer was currently "vague".

McFadden also confirmed that some current benefit claimants would see their current entitlement to benefits reduced when they are reassessed.

But his Conservative counterpart Helen Whately said the idea of legally guaranteeing support "doesn't make sense" and ministers should focus instead on reducing taxes paid by employers.

It comes ahead of a long-awaited review by former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn, which will recommend on Tuesday that under-25s should be guaranteed job placements or training to help them find permanent work.

His report is also expected to say that under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide universal credit - or personal independence payment (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales.

Some could be eligible for a new "additional cost allowance" to cover day-to-day costs related to health conditions, under the plans.

Speaking to Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Milburn said the government should divert money away from the benefits system to boost work support, adding he wanted to see "billions" extra spent on help over the next decade.

However, the idea of reducing the entitlement of existing benefit claimants could prove controversial among Labour MPs, who scuppered a previous benefits-cutting plan under Sir Keir Starmer last year.

Milburn said the reduced entitlement for some should be accompanied by a new "duty on government" to provide jobs support to young people, such as apprenticeships, college places, job coaching, or a job.

He added that the temporary nature of previous job support schemes, including the Kickstart programme during the Covid pandemic, meant that they had been less effective as reducing long-term joblessness.

How the new guarantee would work in practice is not yet clear, with McFadden adding it would have to be "carefully" drafted.

Although local councils have some specific legal duties, including in the areas of child protection and homelessness, duties on central government currently tend to be much broader, such as operating a "comprehensive" health service.

Asked on the same programme whether he agreed with the idea of a guarantee, McFadden said: "I do think we need some legislative underpinning to this."

He added that the offer of support "needs to be more firm," adding: "People need more certainty about what they are entitled to."

He confirmed that the government planned to move younger claimants onto a new benefits system when they undergo scheduled reassessment, and some of them would not receive "what they would get today".

Other claimants, such as those with long-term disabilities, would receive an increased amount, he added.

Also speaking to Kuenssberg, shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said her party backed moves to reduce welfare spending.

But she criticised the proposed legal guarantee of work support, arguing it might "sound a nice thing to do," but ministers would be better off reducing taxes and regulations on businesses to help youngsters find "real jobs".

She added it was "absurd" the government had increased taxes for employers in order to "subsidise things that look like jobs". She added: "Just stop doing the taxing.

Elsewhere in his interview, former health secretary Milburn said:

a sustainable reduction in welfare spending cannot be achieved in two or three years, warning that "crude cuts" to the benefits system would create other additional costs for government

GPs should not be responsible for signing sick notes declaring people unable to work

ministers should "look very carefully" at Labour's manifesto commitment to phase out the reduced minimum wage for those aged 18-21, adding that moves towards this had "imposed a lot of cost" on firms

It comes as the government announced it will further widen eligibly for its scheme that offers jobless under-25s subsidised six-month job roles on the minimum wage.

From next April, eligible claimants will be offered a role after 12 months of unsuccessfully looking for work, rather 18 currently.

It is the second time that eligibility for the scheme has been widened, after the maximum age was increased from 21 to 24 earlier this year.

FinanceTab.title: Bessent Takes Hawkish Turn in White House Debate on China
FinanceTab.text:
President Trump heads to Asia on Monday for high-stakes meetings with foreign leaders aimed at ending Russia’s war in Ukraine and smoothing over trade frictions with China. But the most tense meeting could take place aboard Air Force One.

Sequestered together on the journey across the world will be Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, whose long-running rivalry has recently spilled into the open.

Mr. Lutnick is under fire for slow-walking several measures aimed at clamping down on the supply of Nvidia chips to foreign data centers that serve Chinese clients. The controversy has put Mr. Lutnick at odds with Mr. Bessent, who has increasingly taken a hard line on China. While Mr. Lutnick has pushed for policies more favorable to Nvidia, Mr. Bessent has played the foil, going so far as to call for a dramatic shake-up of the company’s leadership.

The Treasury secretary traditionally manages America’s economic relationship with China. After spending much of last year trying to de-escalate tension between the world’s two largest economies over tariffs, Mr. Bessent has taken a more hawkish stance this year amid growing concern over the artificial intelligence race with China and risks that rogue Chinese A.I. technology could pose to the U.S. economy.

The internal clash over China policy has echoes of Mr. Trump’s first term, when the president’s economic advisers regularly argued about how forcefully to confront China over its trade practices. After Mr. Trump imposed steep tariffs on Chinese imports last year, Mr. Bessent called for de-escalation and helped broker a trade truce that stabilized the global economy.

But in recent months, the Trump administration has been frustrated that China has not lived up to its commitments for purchases of American farm products and to accelerate exports of its critical minerals, which are needed for making high-tech electronics and military equipment.

In a call with Vice Premier He Lifeng of China this month, the Treasury Department said, Mr. Bessent “raised concerns about recent Chinese actions” related to the two nations’ agreement and that “continued progress depends on concrete results.”

“It’s the realization that the original plan or hope with China is not working,” Mr. Pillsbury said, adding that Mr. Bessent was being innovative in the “quest for leverage.”

This month the divide over China policy spilled into public view, after Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was revealed to be having an affair with a woman who led a Singaporean data center firm known as Megaspeed. U.S. intelligence believes the woman is a Chinese intelligence asset. The company is under investigation for allegedly smuggling Nvidia chips to China.

Megaspeed said in a statement that it conducts legitimate and lawful business, and designs its operations to comply with all laws.

When he was asked last week about the U.S. government’s failure to sanction Megaspeed, Mr. Bessent took the unusual step of declaring that he and other officials had long been pushing for action and placed blame on Mr. Lutnick.

“Commerce has the pen,” Mr. Bessent told CNBC. “You will have to ask them about their internal processes.”

On Sunday, Mr. Bessent continued to exert pressure on Nvidia and called on the company to explain itself.

“I want to keep coming back to, what was the culture at Nvidia and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?” Mr. Bessent told Fox News.

In 2025, Mr. Lutnick rolled out several aggressive measures on U.S. technology exports, which prompted Beijing to take countermeasures that stopped the flow of critical minerals to the United States. He has since taken a more cautious stance and warned that broad rules regulating overseas data centers could upset America’s relationship with China and other countries.

On Monday, after months of fierce internal debate, the Commerce Department issued a sweeping rule that will crack down on Chinese companies that have been remotely accessing advanced A.I. chips through data centers in Southeast Asia.

Mr. Lutnick had proposed a softer version that would have had less impact on Nvidia, whose chips are used in overseas data centers. But Mr. Bessent and others in the administration wanted a stronger provision that would clamp down on Chinese access to A.I. computing power.

The Commerce Department, which has authority over the topic, ultimately conceded and published a stronger rule on Monday. But officials drafting the release made clear that it wasn’t their idea.

A news release issued by the Commerce Department said that the new rule was “written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council” — agencies that have both pushed for more stringent rules.

Christopher Padilla, a former Commerce Department official in the Bush administration, said he had never seen the agency publicly disavow responsibility for a rule it was publishing and responsible for enforcing. Only the Commerce Department has the technical expertise or legal authority to write such a rule, he said, but the statement made clear that the agency did not want to issue the rule and did so under duress.

It’s “like open mutiny,” Mr. Padilla said. “That’s unprecedented, and publicly signals a breakdown of interagency cooperation. Not a great signal to send anytime, but especially on the eve of a summit meeting.”

Officials have had limited expectations for the China meetings, which are likely to touch on trade, nuclear weapons and the war in Iran.

In a briefing call on Friday night, administration officials said they did not expect to reach an agreement on nuclear nonproliferation at the summit. They said that the focus of meetings with Xi Jinping, the Chinese leader, and other Chinese officials would be implementing a trade agreement between Washington and Beijing. That would include reducing tariffs and other barriers to trade on each side, and ensuring that China was supplying the United States with rare earth minerals.

In a speech at the National Committee on U.S.-China Relations gala last week, Mr. Bessent said that he was working with his Chinese counterparts to establish an alert system so that the countries could notify each other of serious incidents involving A.I. models. Despite his more hawkish tone, Mr. Bessent said that he did not want to sever economic ties with China.

“As we work toward a more balanced relationship, our objective is to de-risk, not to decouple,” Mr. Bessent said.

For now, Mr. Trump is not publicly taking sides in the rivalry between Mr. Bessent and Mr. Lutnick.

“One view is, you don’t want to insult China,” Mr. Trump said on Monday as he departed for his trip. “The other view is, just go down and dirty and do what you have to do. You can’t say either is wrong or right.”

He added: “I don’t think you want to insult China just before you get there.”

Tony Romm contributed reporting.

FinanceTab.title: Trump Nominates Budget Deputy for Nonpartisan Federal Watchdog Role
FinanceTab.text:
President Trump on Monday nominated Eric M. Ueland, a top deputy at the White House budget office, to serve as the nation’s comptroller general, a move that could hand control of a nonpartisan federal watchdog to one of the administration’s political allies.

If confirmed by the Senate, Mr. Ueland would assume the leadership of the Government Accountability Office, an agency whose responsibilities include monitoring federal spending, identifying government waste and ensuring that the executive branch complies with the wishes of Congress.

The nomination of Mr. Ueland arrived in the waning weeks of Republicans’ majority, and it appeared likely to infuriate Democrats as they prepare to assume control of the House and Senate. The post carries a 15-year term.

Under Mr. Trump, the watchdog known as the G.A.O. has repeatedly uncovered violations of the law at the White House Office of Management and Budget, where Mr. Ueland now serves. The agency has found on multiple occasions that the administration has illegally withheld congressionally enacted funds totaling billions of dollars, violating laws that prohibit the practice known as impoundment.

The problems date back to the president’s first term, when the office concluded in 2020 that the White House wrongly withheld nearly $400 million in military assistance to Ukraine. Congressional Democrats would later cite that finding when they commenced a push to impeach Mr. Trump.

Then, and later in Mr. Trump’s second stint in office, the White House forcefully disputed the G.A.O. and its determinations. It has also worked at times to try to undermine its oversight. Russell T. Vought, the president’s budget director, has frequently attacked the accountability office as partisan, while his aides have recently discouraged federal agencies from responding to its inquiries.

The speculation about Mr. Ueland’s nomination prompted Democratic leaders, Senator Chuck Schumer and Representative Hakeem Jeffries, both of New York, to attack the administration last week for trying to “install a fox in the henhouse.”

The nomination fit a pattern for Mr. Trump, who has looked to install political loyalists across many federal watchdog posts. And it threatened to neuter a unique agency, one that is technically part of the legislative branch, even though the president appoints its leader — with Senate approval.

By law, the G.A.O. also has the power to sue the administration on behalf of lawmakers to force the release of illegally blocked funds. So many ethics groups expressed alarm that the selection of Mr. Ueland, if confirmed, would choke off one of the primary ways that the legislative branch can keep watch over the president.

Unlike other nominations, the appointment of a comptroller general is supposed to happen only after Congress stands up a formal commission to evaluate then submit candidates to the White House. That did not appear to happen with Mr. Ueland.

Instead, Senate Republicans seemed poised to try to confirm Mr. Ueland as soon as possible. He had not even been officially nominated to the post when Senator Rand Paul, Republican of Kentucky and chairman of the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, scheduled a hearing for Thursday on “a nominee” for comptroller general.

The panel did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

FinanceTab.title: Fed Chairman Highlights Economic Uncertainty of A.I. Boom
FinanceTab.text:
Kevin M. Warsh on Monday underscored how uncertain the artificial intelligence boom could be for the economy, highlighting the potential for increased productivity and growth as well as job losses and disappointing stock market returns.

Mr. Warsh’s remarks kicked off a conference at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco that homed in on the work of a task force he established to examine how productivity gains might affect the labor market. It is one of five groups that Mr. Warsh created to look into issues that he has said are central to monetary policy.

Mr. Warsh said that the Fed was modeling scenarios related to how A.I. might impact the economy. Productivity growth had in recent months been “reasonably strong,” he noted, but it “hasn’t yet broken out definitively and structurally to the upside.”

Under the most positive circumstances, the technology could lead “to an increase in productivity and economic gains that are shared broadly ​across labor and the owners of capital,” Mr. Warsh said. In that case, economic growth would rise “persistently above its long-run average” and the unemployment rate would remain steady.

In a gloomier case, Mr. Warsh warned of “substantial labor market disruption” in which jobs are “displaced, rather than complemented” by A.I. In that scenario, the likely outcome would be higher growth but rising unemployment.

Lastly, Mr. Warsh raised the prospect that A.I. returns could disappoint relative to the enormous investment that has flooded into the technology, which has pushed up stock valuations and helped to power consumer spending. At risk in that scenario is an economic slowdown as the broader market falls. Productivity gains are unlikely to accrue against that backdrop, he said.

Mr. Warsh said that the Fed’s role was “neither advocacy nor opposition,” although he conceded that he was “not exactly impartial about American leadership in a time so filled with both challenge and possibility.”

“Our job is to prepare for ​whatever comes next,” ​Mr. Warsh said. “That means contingency planning, which becomes only more important when the world is changing this fast."

Mr. Warsh has in the past argued that higher productivity stemming from A.I. could ultimately slow inflation, which has overshot the Fed’s 2 percent target for nearly six years. So far, continued spending from companies in this space has added to price pressures, especially for crucial components like computer chips and electricity.

Mr. Warsh did not discuss the near-term policy outlook on Monday, but many of his colleagues have in recent weeks explicitly signaled that further interest rate increases will be necessary to get inflation under control. Some have hinted that they would be open to speeding up the pace of those moves by moving at consecutive meetings this winter. The Fed next meets Dec. 8-9 and is widely expected to deliver its second quarter-point increase of the year, a move that will lift borrowing costs to a range of 4 percent to 4.25 percent.

Officials are closely monitoring fluctuations across financial markets, which have whipped around in recent weeks as concerns about the A.I. trade have mounted.

In the Fed’s semiannual financial stability report, released on Friday, nearly 90 percent of survey respondents across Wall Street cited risks related to A.I. as their top concern. They appeared primarily worried about the prospects of disappointing returns leading to a stock market correction as well as cyberattacks.

U.S. stocks sold off sharply on Monday amid a sell-off in A.I. stocks led by Nvidia, the chipmaker whose chief executive Jensen Huang resigned last week after admitting to an affair with a woman whom U.S. officials had identified as a Chinese intelligence asset. The S&P 500 fell roughly 2 percent, while the technology-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped about 2.5 percent.

Mr. Warsh’s visit to the San Francisco Fed was his first to one of the 12 regional banks, the chairman said on Monday. He is scheduled to moderate three panels at the conference, including a fireside chat with Gina Raimondo, who served as secretary of commerce under President Joseph R. Biden Jr., and Marc Andreessen, a venture capitalist.

Mr. Andreessen is one of three external advisers that Mr. Warsh selected to lead the productivity and jobs task force. The others are focused on the Fed’s balance sheet, its communications, how inflation is modeled and the data sources the central bank monitors.

FinanceTab.title: Willie Geist Is Leaving ‘Morning Joe’ After Nearly 20 Years
FinanceTab.text:
Willie Geist, who has been a host of the “Morning Joe” cable news franchise for nearly two decades, said on Monday that he will leave the show at the end of the year to take on an expanded role with NBC News.

Mr. Geist framed his departure as inevitable, as he had been splitting his work life between two networks: MS NOW, the home of “Morning Joe,” and NBC, where he hosts the Sunday edition of the “Today” show and appears in other capacities on the morning program.

That arrangement was easier to manage when the networks were owned by the same parent company, Comcast, and were both operating out of studios at 30 Rockefeller Plaza in Manhattan. MS NOW, then known as MSNBC, was among the cable channels once part of the NBCUniversal TV empire that were spun off under an arrangement formalized earlier this year.

NBC said on Monday that Mr. Geist had been the only on-air employee working for both NBC News and MS NOW since the separation. “It was never intended to last forever,” Mr. Geist said on Monday’s episode of “Morning Joe.”

He said he was leaving “with a very heavy heart, heavy with memories and experiences and friends and family.”

He also addressed his co-hosts, Joe Scarborough and Mika Brzezinski, with whom he had worked since the show premiered in April 2007. “A run that’s lasted nearly 20 years beside the two of you,” he said, had been “the joy of a lifetime, the job of a lifetime.”

There had been an informal understanding that Mr. Geist would stay at MS NOW through the midterm elections, he said. In the spring, he is planning to return for the “Morning Joe” 20th anniversary.

Mr. Geist said on Monday that he was a freelance producer at MSNBC when Mr. Scarborough asked him to be on a political show that he was starting.

After “Morning Joe” debuted, The New York Times described its combination of hard-core political chat and dabs of humor as “unlike anything else on morning television.”

Mr. Scarborough was emotional on Monday’s broadcast. “Just to remind people, we shared our lives together,” he said. Referring to his marriage to Ms. Brzezinski, he added: “Fortunately, you didn’t have to share as much of, you know, of your life with me that Mika’s had to over the past few years. But we’ve shared lives together.”

“And I will say, too, to the corporate overlords, I’m not thrilled,” Mr. Scarborough said.

Ms. Brzezinski told Mr. Geist that she was proud of him. “I’m happy for you,” she said, “but I’m also really sad and not going to hold back on that.”

Ms. Brzezinski and Mr. Scarborough are both under contract with MS NOW through 2029, Axios reported.

Mr. Geist is the son of Bill Geist, a longtime CBS News journalist who was a correspondent with “CBS Sunday Morning” for 31 years. The elder Mr. Geist also wrote the “About New York” column for The Times before joining CBS and is the author of several books.

Willie Geist’s exit from “Morning Joe” will allow for an expanded role at NBC News, where he became a host of the “Today” show’s 9 a.m. hour in 2012 and began hosting the Sunday “Today” show in 2016. He is also a correspondent at NBC News and has contributed to the network’s coverage of the Olympic Games.

FinanceTab.title: Elon Musk Wants to Merge Tesla and SpaceX. Their Businesses Already Overlap.
FinanceTab.text:
Nearly a decade ago, Elon Musk gave Tesla’s design team an unusual assignment: Build a sports car that can fly.

Mr. Musk brought in a small team of engineers from SpaceX, his rocket company, to lend a hand. Led by Bill Riley, SpaceX’s executive overseeing engineering on the rocket intended to land NASA astronauts on the moon, the team juggled their day jobs with outfitting a Roadster sports car with cold-gas thrusters, a technology more commonly found in rockets that has enough force to burst a human eardrum, according to three people familiar with the project.

This year, as engineers from both companies prepared for the car’s debut, they spent months putting it through its paces at SpaceX’s rocket testing facility in McGregor, Texas, the people said. In October, a driverless Roadster did a kick flip in midair, launching off a ramp more than 60 feet high.

This is “what happens when you have a collaboration with the world’s best car company and the world’s best rocket company” Mr. Musk told the crowd.

The flying car demonstration offered a rare glimpse into how the world’s richest person has already created unusual cooperations between his two companies — which he now hopes to merge into a conglomerate valued at more than $3 trillion.

For years, Mr. Musk has quietly shuffled executives and engineers between Tesla and SpaceX to work on his passion projects, blurring the lines between the two, according to interviews with more than a dozen current and former employees, all of whom spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss confidential business matters. The arrangements highlight how Mr. Musk treated the huge companies as interchangeable parts of a single empire, long before shareholders have been asked to vote on combining them.

“It’s unusual because they have a common C.E.O. who is one of the wealthiest people on the planet,” said Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, the senior associate dean for leadership studies at Yale School of Management. “There’s nothing like this that’s happened. Even in the days of John D. Rockefeller, you didn’t have this kind of consolidation of wealth and power.”

Mr. Musk has said the companies’ work overlaps closely and he thinks a merger would be a “good idea.” But he has said he will not be a part of any special committee discussions, comparing the decision to “tap dancing through a minefield.”

Mr. Musk has rapidly consolidated his business empire over the past few years. In February, he merged his A.I. start-up, xAI, with SpaceX, bringing in engineers from the rocket company to lead key projects, including xAI’s data center build out and a reorganization of the start-up, according to five people with knowledge of the company. The acquisition took place less than a year after he merged the A.I. start-up with his social media company, X. The combined SpaceX, which went public in June, is valued at $1.89 trillion.

A merger of Tesla, which is valued at $1.54 trillion, and SpaceX would combine the electrical-vehicle manufacturer and its solar business with a government contractor with ambitions to send astronauts to Mars. The massive deal would wrap cars, rockets, satellites, data centers and A.I. into one company.

“The synergies are pretty obvious,” said Alison Taylor, a clinical associate professor at New York University’s Stern School of Business. “There’s loads of conflicts of interest. They all get resolved with this merger.”

Some of the existing connections between the companies — most of which are paid for by the companies — have been detailed in contracts and public filings. In the prospectus SpaceX’s initial public offering, the company said it had bought about $890 million in Tesla products since 2023, including Cybertrucks and Megapack batteries to help power the company’s data centers. The filing also detailed how the companies share private jets.

Tesla has incorporated some SpaceX products into its offerings, including adding Grok, an A.I. assistant, as a chat feature in Tesla vehicles and incorporating SpaceX’s Starlink satellite service into its future vehicles. Tesla announced in January it had invested $2 billion in xAI as a part of a larger partnership between the two companies.

But much of the overlap can be traced to staffing.

The two companies have shared some talent for more than a decade. Charlie Kuehmann has served as vice president of materials engineering for both companies since 2015. And earlier this year, Tesla’s vice president of A.I., Ashok Elluswamy, the man responsible for leading Tesla’s self-driving software and work on humanoid robotics, began working simultaneously with SpaceX’s A.I. unit, according to two people with knowledge of his work. About one in 22 SpaceX employees list Tesla as a former employer, and the carmaker is SpaceX’s largest source of new hires, according to LinkedIn data from intelligence firm Live Data Technologies. Most came from the car maker’s engineering ranks, and the pace of hiring Tesla recruits has more than doubled this year, the data shows.

Existing staff at both companies have teamed up on projects in addition to the Roadster. Mr. Musk co-founded xAI in 2023 to compete with A.I. start-ups including OpenAI. Soon after, he announced the company had turned an old factory in Memphis into a giant data center called Colossus to help power the Grok chatbot.

Tesla engineers assisted with the project, which took 122 days. Some staff came from Tesla’s own A.I. data center in Texas, a site that helps power the company’s self-driving software, according to three people familiar with the project. Others came from Dojo, Tesla’s supercomputer project meant to compete directly with Nvidia.

In spring 2025, two engineers from Tesla’s Dojo supercomputer team both worked for both xAI and Tesla, according to internal documents viewed by The New York Times. One of them, Dan Rowland, went on to lead xAI’s data center team before leaving the company in August. Those data centers later accounted for $506 million in Tesla battery purchases.

Earlier this year, Mr. Musk moved an xAI project — to create a digital A.I. agent capable of replacing some white-collar workers — to Tesla’s Autopilot team, three people familiar with the project said. Tesla also hired a handful of xAI engineers to work on the A.I. tool, which was renamed Digital Optimus after the company’s humanoid robot, the people said.

Mr. Musk has said the project is part of Tesla’s $2 billion partnership with xAI, which he recently renamed SpaceXSI.

Mr. Musk has also pushed his companies to use the others’ technology. In July, Mr. Musk sent Tesla employees a companywide email asking them to use Grok as their primary A.I. model, according to a memo viewed by The Times. He told staff that the latest Grok model was lower cost compared with competitors like Anthropic, and asked engineers to directly email him with Grok feedback.

Tesla this year gave staff early access to new versions of the Grok chatbot and coding models for testing. SpaceX’s A.I. unit has been using data from Tesla usage to evaluate its A.I. models and hone them, according to internal communications viewed by The Times.

The companies are only continuing to grow closer. In March, Tesla and SpaceX said they were planning a $16.8 billion joint investment in a chip manufacturing facility in Texas. The project will build the chips that help power SpaceX’s A.I., as well as Tesla’s robotics and autonomous vehicle systems. In the months since, the names of dozens of SpaceX engineers showed up listed in Tesla’s internal organizational charts, according to documents viewed by The Times.

Some engineers at Tesla and SpaceX have considered a merger a foregone conclusion for years. Employees have used an internal chat channel dedicated to discussing Tesla’s stock to hype up a potential deal for months, according to three people familiar with the channel.

Mr. Musk has struck a more cautious tone.

“Some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty,” he said last month on a call with investors. “I think that would be overstating it.”

Ryan Mac contributed reporting.

FinanceTab.title: Elon Musk Dreams of Merging Tesla and SpaceX in Move Toward Tech Supremacy
FinanceTab.text:
No one could accuse Elon Musk of thinking small. And the vision he described last month of merging his two companies SpaceX and Tesla is characteristically ambitious: a digital conglomerate of unprecedented scale, spanning rockets, satellites, electric cars, robots and social media.

Mr. Musk is not alone as a digital-age corporate empire builder. Other tech giants are also now sprawling, multi-industry enterprises.

Alphabet’s businesses range well beyond Google search and cloud computing to include video streaming, self-driving cars, drone delivery service and drug development. Amazon has e-commerce, cloud computing, video streaming, a movie studio, robots, warehouses and delivery services.

But a SpaceX-Tesla merger would eclipse the others in its striking array of different businesses, forming a mega-conglomerate worth about $3.5 trillion.

Conglomerates of the past were typically driven by purely financial considerations, like the 1960s merger frenzy on Wall Street, or to diversify a company in order to make it better able to weather economic cycles and international competition, like General Electric.

But today’s conglomerate impulse has a different source — a drive for technological supremacy by broadening a corporation’s market reach and gaining an upper hand in the global A.I. race.

“These big companies are trying to deploy digital technologies, and increasingly artificial intelligence, across industries,” said David Yoffie, a professor at the Harvard Business School.

Mr. Musk acknowledged that the logic of a SpaceX-Tesla merger was a corporate move to seize the A.I. moment. The A.I. businesses at SpaceX include its Grok chatbot and A.I. software models, its data center-building unit and its Cursor A.I. coding assistant. Tesla would bring self-driving cars, robotaxis, humanoid robots and A.I. chip design.

During a SpaceX investor call last month, when Mr. Musk disclosed the two companies were exploring a merger, he said there was “a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity,” the stage at which A.I. surpasses human intelligence.

Corporate conglomerates in America have a rich, colorful and mostly disappointing history. The 1960s saw an explosion of deal making to build the fast-rising conglomerates of their day like ITT Corporation, Litton Industries, Gulf and Western Industries and Ling-Temco-Vought.

These companies were agglomerations of unrelated businesses. ITT (International Telephone and Telegraph) began as an communications company operating outside the United States, but it came to own Avis rental cars, Levitt home builders, Sheraton hotels, Scott’s fertilizer, Wonder Bread and Morton’s frozen foods, among others.

Wall Street was hot. So the currency of acquisition — the buying company’s stock price — was inflated. Debt was cheap and the accounting was creative.

Sleight-of-hand financial deals were the order of the day. One of its foremost practitioners was James Ling — “Jimmy Ling, the merger king.” He started an electrical contracting business in Dallas. Over the years, in deal after deal, he acquired companies in steel manufacturing, meatpacking, car rentals, military aircraft, car rentals, an airline and resorts. At its peak in 1969, LTV, as the company was known, ranked 14th in the Fortune 500.

But the 1960s bull market on Wall Street ended abruptly as inflation rose. LTV’s stock price plummeted, Mr. Ling was ousted and LTV went through a string of bankruptcies.

Still, even after the 1960s conglomerate bubble, there were multi-industry companies that thrived. The leading example grew out of the power generators to lightbulbs conglomerate formed in 1892, when Thomas Edison’s Edison General Electric Company merged with another company.

Throughout the 1980s and 1990s, General Electric enjoyed two decades of prosperity under the leadership of Jack Welch. G.E.’s revenue jumped nearly fivefold, to $130 billion, during Mr. Welch’s tenure. The value of its shares on the stock market soared from $14 billion to more than $410 billion, making G.E. one of the most valuable companies in the world.

In 2000, Fortune magazine named Mr. Welch the “Manager of the Century.”

G.E. seemed proof that a well-run industrial conglomerate could enjoy the advantages of size, funding, shared research and expertise. Like the digital giants of today, G.E. executives spoke of critical industrial technologies — physics and materials science — that could be applied to different industries. A gas turbine power generator, they explained, was essentially a big jet engine bolted to the ground.

For years, the buildup of that business paid off. The company’s finance arm, GE Capital, accounted for up to half of corporate profits in some years and became the largest nonbank financial institution in America. But the 2008 financial crisis hit the division hard.

In 2021, G.E. announced it was splitting into three companies: GE Aerospace, for jet engines; GE Vernova, for power generators and wind power; and GE Healthcare, for medical imaging equipment. The breakup was completed in 2024, as the once-iconic American corporate behemoth bowed to changing times and fortunes.

Studies of conglomerates over the years have found that the stock market value of the combined corporation is typically worth 10 to 15 percent less than if the businesses were stand-alone companies, known as the conglomerate discount. The benefits of combining businesses — the much-praised “synergies” — are overwhelmed by the complexity of managing varied operations and the difficulty of getting a clear picture of the performance of individual businesses.

Skeptics of a SpaceX-Tesla deal point to those challenges. “Shareholders can already own both companies, and this transaction would have all the drawbacks of a conglomerate,” said Baruch Lev, a professor emeritus of accounting and finance at New York University’s Stern School of Business.

Mr. Musk is an experienced corporate acquirer and he has proved skeptics wrong in the past, though a SpaceX-Tesla tie-up would be his largest deal by far. But the merger is not just about corporate size, it is a bet on the “A.I. synergies” that Mr. Musk hopes will result. Much will depend on how much shared A.I. technology and knowledge can be spread across the varied businesses, yielding cost savings and competitive gains, better products and services.

Some analysts say an A.I. conglomerate may well enjoy advantages as the technology is increasingly widely adopted. A combined SpaceX and Tesla, they say, will have greater power to develop, buy and build the technology and deploy it across industry after industry.

They cite the increasing collaboration already between SpaceX and Tesla, led by the giant SpaceX computer chip plant in Texas, announced earlier this year, which will cost at least $55 billion and in total spending could reach $119 billion. Both companies will use the chips manufactured in Texas, with Tesla-designed semiconductors made there as well.

“In this A.I. economy, where computing capacity rules the world, putting SpaceX and Tesla together makes a lot of sense,” said Shay Boloor, chief market strategist at Futurum Equities, an investment research firm.

SportsTab.title: Thomas Frank: How former Spurs boss could restore his reputation and save Crystal Palace
SportsTab.text:
"When the time is right I will look forward to my return as a manager, ready to embrace the job with great energy and dedication," said Thomas Frank in June.

That time is now after the Dane was confirmed as the new manager of Crystal Palace, who are two points and a goal difference deficit away from safety at the bottom of the Premier League.

Former boss Pierre Sage was sacked last week after just 16 league and cup games.

The role offers Frank an opportunity to rebuild his reputation after he was sacked by Tottenham in February after eight months.

Frank described it as "an honour" to be "in charge of this fantastic football club" as Palace announced his arrival on a deal running to June 2029.

"Crystal Palace is an iconic club in England and in the Premier League," Frank told Palace's website.

"I will do everything I possibly can to help and support the players and everyone around the place, and I'm really looking forward to meeting them."

Palace chairman Steve Parish said Frank was the "perfect fit for our club".

But how big is the challenge at Selhurst Park that awaits the man who made his name at Brentford?

"It's going to be a bit of a shock for Thomas Frank," former West Ham and England goalkeeper Rob Green tells BBC Sport.

"He had his success at Brentford - a very well-run club where players are brought in with a lot of thinking and planning to take over the players they sell for profit.

"That doesn't happen at Crystal Palace.

"They lose players and then have a mad scramble to get players in. They have a team that has been decimated by sales and not replaced by the same quality.

"Thomas Frank needs to find something within that team that builds and garners the belief that means that they can compete in the Premier League, because it feels a long way short of that right now."

Will Frank prove the right fit for Palace and haul the Eagles out of the relegation zone?

Since getting the sack at Tottenham after 26 league games last season, Frank has been out of management longer than he was in charge of Spurs.

In the summer he released a statement in which he said "there have been conversations and opportunities" to return to management, but that he had "decided not to rush into the next role".

Frank's name was heavily linked with Palace before they went for a head coach with no Premier League experience to replace Oliver Glasner - the man who delivered an FA Cup, a Conference League title and the Community Shield before moving to Nottingham Forest.

"Palace had one of the best managers they have had, if not forever, silverware coming across the doorstep. Look at what they achieved last season and instead of building on that, they dismantled a team," said former Tottenham and England goalkeeper Paul Robinson.

"They have regressed."

Frank once described managing as being on a "hamster wheel" and a "crazy circus"., external

Palace confirmed his coaching staff will include current assistant manager Paddy McCarthy and goalkeeping coach Andy Quy, who previously worked with him at Brentford.

Justin Cochrane, who is part of Thomas Tuchel's England staff, is set to join.

Palace are also in the process of approaching Chelsea set-piece coach Bernardo Cueva, who would join as assistant first-team coach.

It is understood Frank would like to take Andreas Georgson from Tottenham, though the north London club are determined to keep the Swede.

Denmark fitness coach Chris Haslam, who worked with Frank at Tottenham, is another potential member of Palace's new coaching set-up.

A trip to Coventry City awaits Palace on Saturday.

So why does Frank feel now is the right moment to return to management at a club propping up the table?

Frank, who was part of BBC Sport's World Cup punditry team during the summer, will be coming into the job refreshed and with renewed energy and enthusiasm following several months out of the game.

Between his appointment as Brentford boss in October 2018 and the sack at Tottenham earlier this year, he managed without a break for seven years and four months.

Spending the past few months away from Premier League pressure has allowed Frank, in his own words, to "study, observe and learn from other leaders both within sport and beyond".

Will his positivity and passion rub off on a Palace team who have lost seven times in 10 top-flight matches?

Thomas Frank has a lot of work to do as Crystal Palace have undoubtedly been the worst team in the Premier League so far this season, ranking bottom not just in points (seven) but also goal difference (-14) and expected goal difference (-8.1).

It's the defence where Frank will have to focus most of his attention. Not only have Palace conceded the most goals (24) but they've also faced the most shots (189) and have the worst expected goals against (xGA) figure in the league (21.9).

Their attack has actually not been too bad. While only Hull have taken fewer shots, the Eagles have created really good chances and have perhaps been unlucky not to score a few more goals given the opportunities they've had.

SportsTab.title: Scotland: Andy Robertson caps it all as he takes King Kenny's crown
SportsTab.text:
Andy Robertson has become Scotland's most capped men's international after starting in Monday's Nations League game in Switzerland to reach 103 appearances for his country.

Twelve years on from his debut - off the bench in a Poland friendly - he surpassed his friend and fellow Liverpool legend, Kenny Dalglish, whose record haul had stood for 40 years.

After moving level with the man they - and he - will always call King, the Tottenham Hotspur left-back shifted chat towards the former forward, his commendable humility laid bare.

But, in St Gallen, the spotlight shone on one of Scotland's favourite sons as he moves solo at the summit.

For much of this year, Dalglish was the only man to have pulled on the navy blue of Scotland more times than Robertson.

'King Kenny' topped the list on 102 caps - earning his last in November 1986 against Luxembourg when in a player-manager role at Liverpool.

Few since have even come close to toppling him - and Robertson is keen to stress the throne is still reserved for Dalglish - but it is perhaps fitting it is the current captain, given their great friendship.

Which allows Dalglish to say he's not having any of it.

"He always says: 'You've got millions more games. Nations League, what's that? They didn't have that in my day!'" Robertson joked on the Stick to Football podcast recently.

"I think he might bring up a ratio for years-to-games-played so he's still on top.

"It's obviously something that's been on my radar for a while now. When you get to 80-odd caps, you start to look up."

Dalglish can console himself that his record of 30 goals - held jointly with Denis Law - is safely out of Robertson's reach.

But not out of John McGinn's - the midfielder's double against North Macedonia on Friday took him to within six of the legendary duo.

The Aston Villa captain is lurking only eight caps behind Robertson on the all-time caps list, too, so the Scotland men's centurion club could have three members soon.

Since being given the armband by Alex McLeish after Scott Brown retired in 2018, Robertson has captained Scotland 33 times more than any other player.

At the time, he had earned just 22 caps and was just 24 but had established himself as Liverpool's left-back as they reached the Champions League final.

Now he is the only man to have led Scotland out at three major finals, reaching the milestone at the World Cup this summer.

Scotland and Napoli midfielder Scott McTominay enthused: "He's such a great captain and he's got that good balance between being one of the senior players and saying you need to wake up if you're not playing well.

"Then he's also got the personable side, organising things with the manager, helping young players and stuff. He's brilliant with that, brilliant."

One of those young players is 20-year-old Findlay Curtis, who told the media the night before Robertson's historic night that his captain has "probably been the biggest role model" he's looked up to since joining the international set-up earlier this year.

Perhaps that was because Robertson did him a turn back in the day. Unbeknownst to the skipper.

Rangers winger Curtis was only 14 during the Covid pandemic and was partial to playing a bit of Fifa, and Robertson was a star in his team.

"I was just thinking, I had him in my Fifa team," he explained. "[For] defending and he was just fast as well.

"What a servant he has been for the country."

Over the piece, Robertson's caps are spread fairly evenly among friendlies and qualification games.

Crucially, though, he has also played nine times in major tournaments. What will rankle with him is there is only one win among those nine - June's victory over Haiti in Boston at the World Cup.

Overall, though, Robertson's Scotland career can be characterised by consistency.

He has started 101 of his 103 caps, rarely ever being substituted. He has not missed a camp in three years.

The only question seems to be how many Scotland caps will Robertson end up with?

At 32 and still playing in the Premier League, it appears there will be plenty more to come.
