articles.title: Elon Musk Wants to Merge Tesla and SpaceX. Their Businesses Already Overlap.
articles.text:
Nearly a decade ago, Elon Musk gave Tesla’s design team an unusual assignment: Build a sports car that can fly.

Mr. Musk brought in a small team of engineers from SpaceX, his rocket company, to lend a hand. Led by Bill Riley, SpaceX’s executive overseeing engineering on the rocket intended to land NASA astronauts on the moon, the team juggled their day jobs with outfitting a Roadster sports car with cold-gas thrusters, a technology more commonly found in rockets that has enough force to burst a human eardrum, according to three people familiar with the project.

This year, as engineers from both companies prepared for the car’s debut, they spent months putting it through its paces at SpaceX’s rocket testing facility in McGregor, Texas, the people said. In October, a driverless Roadster did a kick flip in midair, launching off a ramp more than 60 feet high.

This is “what happens when you have a collaboration with the world’s best car company and the world’s best rocket company” Mr. Musk told the crowd.

The flying car demonstration offered a rare glimpse into how the world’s richest person has already created unusual cooperations between his two companies — which he now hopes to merge into a conglomerate valued at more than $3 trillion.

For years, Mr. Musk has quietly shuffled executives and engineers between Tesla and SpaceX to work on his passion projects, blurring the lines between the two, according to interviews with more than a dozen current and former employees, all of whom spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss confidential business matters. The arrangements highlight how Mr. Musk treated the huge companies as interchangeable parts of a single empire, long before shareholders have been asked to vote on combining them.

“It’s unusual because they have a common C.E.O. who is one of the wealthiest people on the planet,” said Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, the senior associate dean for leadership studies at Yale School of Management. “There’s nothing like this that’s happened. Even in the days of John D. Rockefeller, you didn’t have this kind of consolidation of wealth and power.”

Mr. Musk has said the companies’ work overlaps closely and he thinks a merger would be a “good idea.” But he has said he will not be a part of any special committee discussions, comparing the decision to “tap dancing through a minefield.”

Mr. Musk has rapidly consolidated his business empire over the past few years. In February, he merged his A.I. start-up, xAI, with SpaceX, bringing in engineers from the rocket company to lead key projects, including xAI’s data center build out and a reorganization of the start-up, according to five people with knowledge of the company. The acquisition took place less than a year after he merged the A.I. start-up with his social media company, X. The combined SpaceX, which went public in June, is valued at $1.89 trillion.

A merger of Tesla, which is valued at $1.54 trillion, and SpaceX would combine the electrical-vehicle manufacturer and its solar business with a government contractor with ambitions to send astronauts to Mars. The massive deal would wrap cars, rockets, satellites, data centers and A.I. into one company.

“The synergies are pretty obvious,” said Alison Taylor, a clinical associate professor at New York University’s Stern School of Business. “There’s loads of conflicts of interest. They all get resolved with this merger.”

Some of the existing connections between the companies — most of which are paid for by the companies — have been detailed in contracts and public filings. In the prospectus SpaceX’s initial public offering, the company said it had bought about $890 million in Tesla products since 2023, including Cybertrucks and Megapack batteries to help power the company’s data centers. The filing also detailed how the companies share private jets.

Tesla has incorporated some SpaceX products into its offerings, including adding Grok, an A.I. assistant, as a chat feature in Tesla vehicles and incorporating SpaceX’s Starlink satellite service into its future vehicles. Tesla announced in January it had invested $2 billion in xAI as a part of a larger partnership between the two companies.

But much of the overlap can be traced to staffing.

The two companies have shared some talent for more than a decade. Charlie Kuehmann has served as vice president of materials engineering for both companies since 2015. And earlier this year, Tesla’s vice president of A.I., Ashok Elluswamy, the man responsible for leading Tesla’s self-driving software and work on humanoid robotics, began working simultaneously with SpaceX’s A.I. unit, according to two people with knowledge of his work. About one in 22 SpaceX employees list Tesla as a former employer, and the carmaker is SpaceX’s largest source of new hires, according to LinkedIn data from intelligence firm Live Data Technologies. Most came from the car maker’s engineering ranks, and the pace of hiring Tesla recruits has more than doubled this year, the data shows.

Existing staff at both companies have teamed up on projects in addition to the Roadster. Mr. Musk co-founded xAI in 2023 to compete with A.I. start-ups including OpenAI. Soon after, he announced the company had turned an old factory in Memphis into a giant data center called Colossus to help power the Grok chatbot.

Tesla engineers assisted with the project, which took 122 days. Some staff came from Tesla’s own A.I. data center in Texas, a site that helps power the company’s self-driving software, according to three people familiar with the project. Others came from Dojo, Tesla’s supercomputer project meant to compete directly with Nvidia.

In spring 2025, two engineers from Tesla’s Dojo supercomputer team both worked for both xAI and Tesla, according to internal documents viewed by The New York Times. One of them, Dan Rowland, went on to lead xAI’s data center team before leaving the company in August. Those data centers later accounted for $506 million in Tesla battery purchases.

Earlier this year, Mr. Musk moved an xAI project — to create a digital A.I. agent capable of replacing some white-collar workers — to Tesla’s Autopilot team, three people familiar with the project said. Tesla also hired a handful of xAI engineers to work on the A.I. tool, which was renamed Digital Optimus after the company’s humanoid robot, the people said.

Mr. Musk has said the project is part of Tesla’s $2 billion partnership with xAI, which he recently renamed SpaceXSI.

Mr. Musk has also pushed his companies to use the others’ technology. In July, Mr. Musk sent Tesla employees a companywide email asking them to use Grok as their primary A.I. model, according to a memo viewed by The Times. He told staff that the latest Grok model was lower cost compared with competitors like Anthropic, and asked engineers to directly email him with Grok feedback.

Tesla this year gave staff early access to new versions of the Grok chatbot and coding models for testing. SpaceX’s A.I. unit has been using data from Tesla usage to evaluate its A.I. models and hone them, according to internal communications viewed by The Times.

The companies are only continuing to grow closer. In March, Tesla and SpaceX said they were planning a $16.8 billion joint investment in a chip manufacturing facility in Texas. The project will build the chips that help power SpaceX’s A.I., as well as Tesla’s robotics and autonomous vehicle systems. In the months since, the names of dozens of SpaceX engineers showed up listed in Tesla’s internal organizational charts, according to documents viewed by The Times.

Some engineers at Tesla and SpaceX have considered a merger a foregone conclusion for years. Employees have used an internal chat channel dedicated to discussing Tesla’s stock to hype up a potential deal for months, according to three people familiar with the channel.

Mr. Musk has struck a more cautious tone.

“Some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty,” he said last month on a call with investors. “I think that would be overstating it.”

Ryan Mac contributed reporting.

articles.title: Elon Musk Dreams of Merging Tesla and SpaceX in Move Toward Tech Supremacy
articles.text:
No one could accuse Elon Musk of thinking small. And the vision he described last month of merging his two companies SpaceX and Tesla is characteristically ambitious: a digital conglomerate of unprecedented scale, spanning rockets, satellites, electric cars, robots and social media.

Mr. Musk is not alone as a digital-age corporate empire builder. Other tech giants are also now sprawling, multi-industry enterprises.

Alphabet’s businesses range well beyond Google search and cloud computing to include video streaming, self-driving cars, drone delivery service and drug development. Amazon has e-commerce, cloud computing, video streaming, a movie studio, robots, warehouses and delivery services.

But a SpaceX-Tesla merger would eclipse the others in its striking array of different businesses, forming a mega-conglomerate worth about $3.5 trillion.

Conglomerates of the past were typically driven by purely financial considerations, like the 1960s merger frenzy on Wall Street, or to diversify a company in order to make it better able to weather economic cycles and international competition, like General Electric.

But today’s conglomerate impulse has a different source — a drive for technological supremacy by broadening a corporation’s market reach and gaining an upper hand in the global A.I. race.

“These big companies are trying to deploy digital technologies, and increasingly artificial intelligence, across industries,” said David Yoffie, a professor at the Harvard Business School.

Mr. Musk acknowledged that the logic of a SpaceX-Tesla merger was a corporate move to seize the A.I. moment. The A.I. businesses at SpaceX include its Grok chatbot and A.I. software models, its data center-building unit and its Cursor A.I. coding assistant. Tesla would bring self-driving cars, robotaxis, humanoid robots and A.I. chip design.

During a SpaceX investor call last month, when Mr. Musk disclosed the two companies were exploring a merger, he said there was “a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity,” the stage at which A.I. surpasses human intelligence.

Corporate conglomerates in America have a rich, colorful and mostly disappointing history. The 1960s saw an explosion of deal making to build the fast-rising conglomerates of their day like ITT Corporation, Litton Industries, Gulf and Western Industries and Ling-Temco-Vought.

These companies were agglomerations of unrelated businesses. ITT (International Telephone and Telegraph) began as an communications company operating outside the United States, but it came to own Avis rental cars, Levitt home builders, Sheraton hotels, Scott’s fertilizer, Wonder Bread and Morton’s frozen foods, among others.

Wall Street was hot. So the currency of acquisition — the buying company’s stock price — was inflated. Debt was cheap and the accounting was creative.

Sleight-of-hand financial deals were the order of the day. One of its foremost practitioners was James Ling — “Jimmy Ling, the merger king.” He started an electrical contracting business in Dallas. Over the years, in deal after deal, he acquired companies in steel manufacturing, meatpacking, car rentals, military aircraft, car rentals, an airline and resorts. At its peak in 1969, LTV, as the company was known, ranked 14th in the Fortune 500.

But the 1960s bull market on Wall Street ended abruptly as inflation rose. LTV’s stock price plummeted, Mr. Ling was ousted and LTV went through a string of bankruptcies.

Still, even after the 1960s conglomerate bubble, there were multi-industry companies that thrived. The leading example grew out of the power generators to lightbulbs conglomerate formed in 1892, when Thomas Edison’s Edison General Electric Company merged with another company.

Throughout the 1980s and 1990s, General Electric enjoyed two decades of prosperity under the leadership of Jack Welch. G.E.’s revenue jumped nearly fivefold, to $130 billion, during Mr. Welch’s tenure. The value of its shares on the stock market soared from $14 billion to more than $410 billion, making G.E. one of the most valuable companies in the world.

In 2000, Fortune magazine named Mr. Welch the “Manager of the Century.”

G.E. seemed proof that a well-run industrial conglomerate could enjoy the advantages of size, funding, shared research and expertise. Like the digital giants of today, G.E. executives spoke of critical industrial technologies — physics and materials science — that could be applied to different industries. A gas turbine power generator, they explained, was essentially a big jet engine bolted to the ground.

For years, the buildup of that business paid off. The company’s finance arm, GE Capital, accounted for up to half of corporate profits in some years and became the largest nonbank financial institution in America. But the 2008 financial crisis hit the division hard.

In 2021, G.E. announced it was splitting into three companies: GE Aerospace, for jet engines; GE Vernova, for power generators and wind power; and GE Healthcare, for medical imaging equipment. The breakup was completed in 2024, as the once-iconic American corporate behemoth bowed to changing times and fortunes.

Studies of conglomerates over the years have found that the stock market value of the combined corporation is typically worth 10 to 15 percent less than if the businesses were stand-alone companies, known as the conglomerate discount. The benefits of combining businesses — the much-praised “synergies” — are overwhelmed by the complexity of managing varied operations and the difficulty of getting a clear picture of the performance of individual businesses.

Skeptics of a SpaceX-Tesla deal point to those challenges. “Shareholders can already own both companies, and this transaction would have all the drawbacks of a conglomerate,” said Baruch Lev, a professor emeritus of accounting and finance at New York University’s Stern School of Business.

Mr. Musk is an experienced corporate acquirer and he has proved skeptics wrong in the past, though a SpaceX-Tesla tie-up would be his largest deal by far. But the merger is not just about corporate size, it is a bet on the “A.I. synergies” that Mr. Musk hopes will result. Much will depend on how much shared A.I. technology and knowledge can be spread across the varied businesses, yielding cost savings and competitive gains, better products and services.

Some analysts say an A.I. conglomerate may well enjoy advantages as the technology is increasingly widely adopted. A combined SpaceX and Tesla, they say, will have greater power to develop, buy and build the technology and deploy it across industry after industry.

They cite the increasing collaboration already between SpaceX and Tesla, led by the giant SpaceX computer chip plant in Texas, announced earlier this year, which will cost at least $55 billion and in total spending could reach $119 billion. Both companies will use the chips manufactured in Texas, with Tesla-designed semiconductors made there as well.

“In this A.I. economy, where computing capacity rules the world, putting SpaceX and Tesla together makes a lot of sense,” said Shay Boloor, chief market strategist at Futurum Equities, an investment research firm.

articles.title: Thomas Frank: How former Spurs boss could restore his reputation and save Crystal Palace
articles.text:
"When the time is right I will look forward to my return as a manager, ready to embrace the job with great energy and dedication," said Thomas Frank in June.

That time is now after the Dane was confirmed as the new manager of Crystal Palace, who are two points and a goal difference deficit away from safety at the bottom of the Premier League.

Former boss Pierre Sage was sacked last week after just 16 league and cup games.

The role offers Frank an opportunity to rebuild his reputation after he was sacked by Tottenham in February after eight months.

Frank described it as "an honour" to be "in charge of this fantastic football club" as Palace announced his arrival on a deal running to June 2029.

"Crystal Palace is an iconic club in England and in the Premier League," Frank told Palace's website.

"I will do everything I possibly can to help and support the players and everyone around the place, and I'm really looking forward to meeting them."

Palace chairman Steve Parish said Frank was the "perfect fit for our club".

But how big is the challenge at Selhurst Park that awaits the man who made his name at Brentford?

"It's going to be a bit of a shock for Thomas Frank," former West Ham and England goalkeeper Rob Green tells BBC Sport.

"He had his success at Brentford - a very well-run club where players are brought in with a lot of thinking and planning to take over the players they sell for profit.

"That doesn't happen at Crystal Palace.

"They lose players and then have a mad scramble to get players in. They have a team that has been decimated by sales and not replaced by the same quality.

"Thomas Frank needs to find something within that team that builds and garners the belief that means that they can compete in the Premier League, because it feels a long way short of that right now."

Will Frank prove the right fit for Palace and haul the Eagles out of the relegation zone?

Since getting the sack at Tottenham after 26 league games last season, Frank has been out of management longer than he was in charge of Spurs.

In the summer he released a statement in which he said "there have been conversations and opportunities" to return to management, but that he had "decided not to rush into the next role".

Frank's name was heavily linked with Palace before they went for a head coach with no Premier League experience to replace Oliver Glasner - the man who delivered an FA Cup, a Conference League title and the Community Shield before moving to Nottingham Forest.

"Palace had one of the best managers they have had, if not forever, silverware coming across the doorstep. Look at what they achieved last season and instead of building on that, they dismantled a team," said former Tottenham and England goalkeeper Paul Robinson.

"They have regressed."

Frank once described managing as being on a "hamster wheel" and a "crazy circus"., external

Palace confirmed his coaching staff will include current assistant manager Paddy McCarthy and goalkeeping coach Andy Quy, who previously worked with him at Brentford.

Justin Cochrane, who is part of Thomas Tuchel's England staff, is set to join.

Palace are also in the process of approaching Chelsea set-piece coach Bernardo Cueva, who would join as assistant first-team coach.

It is understood Frank would like to take Andreas Georgson from Tottenham, though the north London club are determined to keep the Swede.

Denmark fitness coach Chris Haslam, who worked with Frank at Tottenham, is another potential member of Palace's new coaching set-up.

A trip to Coventry City awaits Palace on Saturday.

So why does Frank feel now is the right moment to return to management at a club propping up the table?

Frank, who was part of BBC Sport's World Cup punditry team during the summer, will be coming into the job refreshed and with renewed energy and enthusiasm following several months out of the game.

Between his appointment as Brentford boss in October 2018 and the sack at Tottenham earlier this year, he managed without a break for seven years and four months.

Spending the past few months away from Premier League pressure has allowed Frank, in his own words, to "study, observe and learn from other leaders both within sport and beyond".

Will his positivity and passion rub off on a Palace team who have lost seven times in 10 top-flight matches?

Thomas Frank has a lot of work to do as Crystal Palace have undoubtedly been the worst team in the Premier League so far this season, ranking bottom not just in points (seven) but also goal difference (-14) and expected goal difference (-8.1).

It's the defence where Frank will have to focus most of his attention. Not only have Palace conceded the most goals (24) but they've also faced the most shots (189) and have the worst expected goals against (xGA) figure in the league (21.9).

Their attack has actually not been too bad. While only Hull have taken fewer shots, the Eagles have created really good chances and have perhaps been unlucky not to score a few more goals given the opportunities they've had.

articles.title: Scotland: Andy Robertson caps it all as he takes King Kenny's crown
articles.text:
Andy Robertson has become Scotland's most capped men's international after starting in Monday's Nations League game in Switzerland to reach 103 appearances for his country.

Twelve years on from his debut - off the bench in a Poland friendly - he surpassed his friend and fellow Liverpool legend, Kenny Dalglish, whose record haul had stood for 40 years.

After moving level with the man they - and he - will always call King, the Tottenham Hotspur left-back shifted chat towards the former forward, his commendable humility laid bare.

But, in St Gallen, the spotlight shone on one of Scotland's favourite sons as he moves solo at the summit.

For much of this year, Dalglish was the only man to have pulled on the navy blue of Scotland more times than Robertson.

'King Kenny' topped the list on 102 caps - earning his last in November 1986 against Luxembourg when in a player-manager role at Liverpool.

Few since have even come close to toppling him - and Robertson is keen to stress the throne is still reserved for Dalglish - but it is perhaps fitting it is the current captain, given their great friendship.

Which allows Dalglish to say he's not having any of it.

"He always says: 'You've got millions more games. Nations League, what's that? They didn't have that in my day!'" Robertson joked on the Stick to Football podcast recently.

"I think he might bring up a ratio for years-to-games-played so he's still on top.

"It's obviously something that's been on my radar for a while now. When you get to 80-odd caps, you start to look up."

Dalglish can console himself that his record of 30 goals - held jointly with Denis Law - is safely out of Robertson's reach.

But not out of John McGinn's - the midfielder's double against North Macedonia on Friday took him to within six of the legendary duo.

The Aston Villa captain is lurking only eight caps behind Robertson on the all-time caps list, too, so the Scotland men's centurion club could have three members soon.

Since being given the armband by Alex McLeish after Scott Brown retired in 2018, Robertson has captained Scotland 33 times more than any other player.

At the time, he had earned just 22 caps and was just 24 but had established himself as Liverpool's left-back as they reached the Champions League final.

Now he is the only man to have led Scotland out at three major finals, reaching the milestone at the World Cup this summer.

Scotland and Napoli midfielder Scott McTominay enthused: "He's such a great captain and he's got that good balance between being one of the senior players and saying you need to wake up if you're not playing well.

"Then he's also got the personable side, organising things with the manager, helping young players and stuff. He's brilliant with that, brilliant."

One of those young players is 20-year-old Findlay Curtis, who told the media the night before Robertson's historic night that his captain has "probably been the biggest role model" he's looked up to since joining the international set-up earlier this year.

Perhaps that was because Robertson did him a turn back in the day. Unbeknownst to the skipper.

Rangers winger Curtis was only 14 during the Covid pandemic and was partial to playing a bit of Fifa, and Robertson was a star in his team.

"I was just thinking, I had him in my Fifa team," he explained. "[For] defending and he was just fast as well.

"What a servant he has been for the country."

Over the piece, Robertson's caps are spread fairly evenly among friendlies and qualification games.

Crucially, though, he has also played nine times in major tournaments. What will rankle with him is there is only one win among those nine - June's victory over Haiti in Boston at the World Cup.

Overall, though, Robertson's Scotland career can be characterised by consistency.

He has started 101 of his 103 caps, rarely ever being substituted. He has not missed a camp in three years.

The only question seems to be how many Scotland caps will Robertson end up with?

At 32 and still playing in the Premier League, it appears there will be plenty more to come.

articles.title: Has James Trafford replaced Jordan Pickford as England No 1?
articles.text:
It was some night for James Trafford.

As he was mobbed by his England team-mates for a late double save that secured a memorable 3-2 win against world champions Spain, the debate that followed about who the country's number one is was inevitable.

The Leeds keeper was given his chance to show England boss Thomas Tuchel what he could do again - and he absolutely took it.

On his fifth England cap the 24-year-old enjoyed a magnificent performance in Madrid as his side handed the hosts their first loss in 43 matches.

Trafford made four key saves in the final 12 minutes of the game, including an incredible double stop to first deny a Lamine Yamal curler and then dive again to his right to keep out Fermin Lopez from close range.

Last week Tuchel had made it clear that Everton goalkeeper Jordan Pickford was his number one.

But after full-time in Spain Tuchel told ITV Sport "there's no number one" and Trafford had "a brilliant match".

So, following his performance on Sunday night, is Trafford now likely to oust Pickford as England's go-to goalkeeper?

Despite being just 24 years old Trafford has already been England's most expensive goalkeeper by transfer fee... twice.

Trafford returned to his boyhood Manchester City from Burnley for a £31m fee in 2025 and then left the Etihad for Leeds for £45m this summer - having been limited to being Pep Guardiola's 'cup goalkeeper'.

Given the downturn in form of their current goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma, many City fans may well be wishing Trafford had stayed. Their loss is Leeds' - and maybe England's - gain.

At Leeds he has found his form and this season ranks first among the 52 goalkeepers who have played at least 10 games in Europe's big five leagues by save percentage (81.4%).

He has made five appearances for England, all of them in 2026, and has rotated with Pickford across the Three Lions' five matches since the World Cup.

Pickford has started against Czech Republic and Croatia twice whereas Trafford has played against Czech Republic and started both England's matches with Spain, home and away.

After England's win in Madrid, which was the first time Spain had lost in the city in 39 years, Trafford's double-save was praised by his Three Lions team-mate Declan Rice.

"Everything happened so quick so for him to make two in the space of two seconds is massive," he told ITV. "A massive night for him."

Spain manager Luis de la Fuente agreed. He said: "We did generate some chances but England's goalkeeper has produced a fantastic performance and stopped two or three potential goals in the last 10 or 15 minutes."

After the double-save several England players ran over to celebrate with Trafford.

And on Tuchel's decision to rotate between his two keepers former Manchester United captain Roy Keane told ITV: "I think it's smart management.

"This is the perfect time for Trafford to come in, against top players, and show what he's capable of doing."

Social media has been full of the 'England number one' debate since, with many suggesting this was a moment that marked the changing of the guard.

Could Tuchel really now not start with Trafford for England's Nations League quarter-finals? Only time will tell.

What about Pickford though? England's undisputed first choice for almost 10 years has rarely let his country down.

The 32-year-old has won 94 caps for England since making his debut in a 0-0 draw with Germany in 2017 and during his time as number one England have reached two World Cup semi-finals and two Euros finals.

According to Opta stats, Pickford has only made two errors leading to goals across his England career, with 46 clean sheets and a 74.3% save ratio.

And since the start of the 2024-25 season, only Arsenal's title-winning keeper David Raya has more clean sheets in the league than Pickford at Everton.

"We saw the last selections and all thought Jordan Pickford's place is under threat and James Trafford is going to be the next number one. I don't think Thomas Tuchel saw it as starkly or simply as that," said former England number one goalkeeper Paul Robinson to BBC Sport before England's win against Spain,

"It's a conversation that will definitely take place down the road, but not now. Jordan is England's first choice, in my opinion, rightfully so given his consistency and performances over such a long period.

"This is a debate and conversation for the future definitely because Father Time catches up with everyone eventually and the manager needs to have a contingency plan, but Jordan Pickford very much remains number one and Thomas Tuchel has said as much.

"I don't think Jordan Pickford is under threat for his jersey on a permanent basis any time soon, irrespective of the next selection."

This isn't a debate that is going away any time soon. But having two goalkeepers genuinely competing for that number one shirt can only be to England's benefit.

articles.title: Nations Championship: England's Will Joseph in line to start against New Zealand
articles.text:
England's Will Joseph is in line to retain his place for Saturday's blockbuster Nations Championship meeting with New Zealand after scoring five tries against Japan.

In the absence of the injured Immanuel Feyi-Waboso, Joseph is understood to be in pole position to reprise his role on the wing after a performance packed with pace and finishing ability.

Joseph scored a hat-trick inside the first 19 minutes, on the way to becoming only the fifth England men's player to score five tries in one match.

He also headed the team's charts for metres carried (224) and top speed (21.7mph).

The 24-year-old won his second Test cap in Saturday's 78-15 thrashing of the Brave Blossoms, four and half years after making his debut as a teenager.

After a late cameo as a replacement in England's second Test win over Australia in July 2022, Joseph struggled to fulfil his promise. Boyhood club London Irish went into liquidation and a stint at Harlequins was hampered by injury and a lack of game time.

However, Joseph has been a key part of Gloucester's resurgence this season and, watched by elder brother and former England centre Jonathan Joseph, he made a sensational return to international rugby at Allianz Stadium last weekend.

articles.title: Jurgen Klopp says Fifa president Gianni Infantino worse than predecessor Sepp Blatter
articles.text:
Germany head coach Jurgen Klopp says he "didn't think things could get worse after Sepp Blatter, but someone has managed to do just that" as he called for Fifa president Gianni Infantino to be replaced.

Blatter resigned as Fifa boss in 2015 amid a corruption scandal and was succeeded by Infantino in February 2016.

Infantino plans to stand for re-election in March but has been under pressure since scrapping his Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal, which included selling off stakes in the World Cup and other Fifa competitions to private investors.

Infantino apologised to the Fifa Council for the plan but was told he was not fit to lead world football's governing body unless he released all the documents and answered key questions.

"I've been following football for many years. There are people who are much more knowledgeable about this than I am. But I think most people now agree a change would make a lot of sense," said former Liverpool boss Klopp.

"I didn't think things could get worse after Sepp Blatter, but someone has managed to do just that."

Klopp added: "Regarding Gianni Infantino, surely the next person to come along can do a better job."

French Football Federation (FFF) president Philippe Diallo has been named as Uefa's candidate to challenge Infantino.

Diallo received the unanimous support of Uefa's executive committee and formal ratification from the FFF is expected on Tuesday.

Uefa, which is European football's governing body, said it has "full confidence" Diallo would "uphold the highest standards of governance" amid its calls for "renewed unity and trust within the global football community".

articles.title: Jim Ratcliffe's Ineos group settles £180m boat claim with Ben Ainslie's Athena Racing
articles.text:
Sir Jim Ratcliffe's Ineos group has settled a High Court claim with Sir Ben Ainslie's Athena Racing over a £180m boat used in the America's Cup.

Ineos took legal steps against Athena Racing in March to secure the return of the boat - named Britannia - after alleging Ainslie's firm had breached a deal between the two companies.

Ratcliffe's petrochemicals company funded two America's Cup cycles led by four-time Olympic champion Ainslie in Auckland in 2021 and Barcelona two years ago.

However, relations between the Manchester United co-owner and Ainslie reportedly turned sour and they split in January 2025, with plans to challenge for the 38th America's Cup in Naples in 2027 abandoned three months later.

In a statement on Monday, an Ineos spokesperson said they had reached a settlement with Athena Racing and "considers the matter now closed".

Meanwhile, Athena confirmed the team has ownership of the multimillion-pound boat. "Athena Racing/GB1 have always been, and remain, the owners of their assets," a statement read.

Ineos blamed the decision to split with Athena on "a protracted negotiation", claiming Ainslie's team had caused a costly six-month delay to settlement talks.

Ainslie became Ineos Britannia's team principal and skipper when he received the backing of Britain's largest privately-owned company in 2018 in a bid to win sailing's oldest prize - something Great Britain had never done before.

In 2024, the team led by Ainslie, 49, reached the final of the 37th edition in Barcelona for the first time since 1964, but they were beaten 7-2 by defending champions New Zealand.

Following the fallout with Ratcliffe, Ainslie secured private equity funding for Athena from Oakley Capital and rebranded the team as GB1 in January.

articles.title: ATP Finals: Carlos Alcaraz begins title bid with statement win over Frances Tiafoe
articles.text:
Carlos Alcaraz was at his scintillating best as his quest for a first ATP Finals triumph began with a statement victory over Frances Tiafoe.

Afterwards, the Spaniard warned his rivals that he has never felt better at this stage of the season.

Alcaraz hit 21 winners and made just nine unforced errors in a blistering 69-minute performance as he dismantled world number eight Tiafoe 6-2 6-2.

The seven-time major winner is on a 10-match winning streak following back-to-back titles in Vienna and Paris as he continues his remarkable return following a four-month wrist injury lay-off.

He has won three titles and lost just twice in 23 matches since making his return at the US Open in August.

"This is the best that I felt so far in my career at this part of the season," said the former world number one.

"I'm really happy with everything that I've done. I have obviously never experienced something like this year.

"It was unusual for me to have a lot of months out of competition and it means I'm coming here with a lot of energy and ambition."

Alcaraz reached the title match at the ATP Finals - the season-ending tournament featuring the year's eight top-performing men's players - for the first time last year.

On that occasion, he was beaten by main rival Jannik Sinner.

Having returned to full fitness, and with Sinner absent through injury, Alcaraz provided an immediate, ominous warning to his opponents on his return to Turin.

The 23-year-old lost just a single point on his serve and made only two unforced errors as he captured the first set in a devastating opening 27 minutes.

Tiafoe did not do an awful lot wrong, but the US Open semi-finalist was often left staring in bewilderment in response to his opponent's level.

The American maintained a first-serve average of 74%, but he was not able to win a single point on his second serve (0/12) during the match.

Dominant from the baseline, Alcaraz also dazzled with his athleticism and shot-making, while he showed necessary grit to deny Tiafoe three break points at 3-2 in the second set.

It was a performance scored as a 9.6 out of 10 by the ATP Performance Rating, which combines several statistics to measure a player's overall game.

"The trouble that I got every time I have played against Frances made me really focused," said Alcaraz, whose two most recent meetings with Tiafoe had come at Grand Slams and went to five sets.

"I prepared the match tactically really well. I wanted to let him know it was going to be a great battle if he wanted to win.

"I'm just really happy to start the tournament like this."

Home favourite Flavio Cobolli begins his tournament against Daniil Medevedev in the other Ivan Lendl Group match later on Monday.

articles.title: Cristiano Ronaldo: Portugal boss Jorge Jesus responds to criticism from Ronaldo's mother
articles.text:
Jorge Jesus has responded to claims by Cristiano Ronaldo's mother, Dolores Aveiro, that her son had been "deceived" by the Portugal manager.

Ronaldo, 41, retired from international football on 5 November, ending a career with his country during which he won 234 caps and scored 146 goals.

But his retirement also came less than a month after he had been given a 30-day suspension and fined £215 for walking out of the Portugal camp in September after being told he would not start the Nations League match against Denmark.

Portugal played their first game since Ronaldo's announcement against the Danes on Saturday, losing 4-1 at home.

While attending a Sporting event on Monday, Aveiro was asked about Ronaldo's national team retirement, and said:, external "Of course he was sad.

"They deceived him. And I'm sad, too. The defeat [against Denmark] was well-deserved. I was actually glad."

Before Portugal's Nations League game against Wales in Cardiff on Tuesday (19:45 GMT), Jesus was asked for his thoughts on Aveiro's comments.

"Now I have to respond to Cristiano Ronaldo's mother?" he said.

"She is a lady I greatly respect - she suffered a lot to raise her children."

Asked if the debate about Ronaldo's international retirement would end, Jesus added: "I don't know when it's going to stop.

"If you guys ask the questions, I have to answer. If you ask about Ronaldo next year, I will answer."

articles.title: England v New Zealand: All Blacks coach Dave Rennie says team 'let the country down' in Wales defeat
articles.text:
New Zealand head coach Dave Rennie has demanded a reaction against England on Saturday after saying the All Blacks "let the country down" in their historic defeat by Wales.

In one of the great upsets of the professional era, New Zealand lost 35-28 in Cardiff at the weekend, a first defeat against the Welsh in 73 years.

New Zealand will face an in-form England in Twickenham as they look to avoid back-to-back Nations Championship losses, with Rennie vowing not to brush the Wales result "under the carpet".

"It's important we poke each other in the chest at the start of the week," Rennie said.

"You have to front up and take things on the chin, all of us. Come Saturday, our mindset will be fully on England and our job is to perform.

"We will be highly motivated for the weekend, but we won't brush the [Wales] result under the carpet.

"[The players] are feeling it. They know we let ourselves down and we let the country down."

Rennie paid tribute to a "clinical and passionate" Wales team, but he lamented his side's uncharacteristic wastefulness when camped in Welsh territory in the final quarter of the game.

"We are all reflecting on what we could do better. You can't just blame it on the guys who take the field," Rennie said.

"It's disappointing and not good enough, but we've got to learn from it and bottle up the feeling post-game, because it hurts, and we have some pretty big footy coming up in the next few weeks and next year.

"I should have done a better job last week. We picked a side that was a very good side and a side I was really confident that if we played to our potential would perform well.

"But I also knew [Wales] had a really strong coaching group, smart, and were a passionate nation playing at home."

Rennie is set to call upon a host of big-name players for the match at Allianz Stadium as the All Blacks look to avenge their defeat in Twickenham this time last year.

Damian McKenzie, Jordie Barrett, Codie Taylor and Cam Roigard will all return, while star wing Will Jordan is in the selection mix after a hamstring problem.

However, Quinn Tupaea, a fixture in the team throughout 2026 at outside centre, needs surgery on a thumb injury and will be out for the next 10 weeks.

"Playing England at Twickenham is always a big occasion, and we are playing a side who is in good form," added Rennie.

"They can hurt you up front, they bring a lot of line speed defensively, and they've been really sharp attack-wise. They are playing a lot of footy and we are well aware of that.

"The loss on the weekend creates a little bit more edge, but I wouldn't say we are going to be more motivated than we would have been. England at Twickenham is always a tough assignment."

articles.title: James Botham: Wales' unlikely hero in historic win over New Zealand
articles.text:
James Botham lay sprawled on the Principality Stadium turf, pain and exhaustion etched across his face.

Whenever the whistle blew, the Wales flanker in the red scrum cap took an age to rise. Precious seconds to recover. Nobody counts tackles when the ball is dead.

But when play resumed, he was everywhere. Tackling, scrambling, hitting the deck and springing back up.

By the final whistle, Botham had helped Wales beat New Zealand for the first time in 73 years. He was man of the match. And as the celebrations began, the tears flowed.

Quite an afternoon for a player accustomed to working away from the spotlight.

Keeping a Botham out of the headlines was always going to be difficult.

His grandfather, Lord Ian Botham, is one of Britain's great sporting celebrities. Outspoken, charismatic and capable of turning cricket matches almost single-handedly, he is box-office.

James is different.

His game is built on tackles, chasing, wrestling and relentless graft. Few positions in rugby are less glamorous than blind-side flanker.

But on Saturday, Wales' number six was the star of the show.

Botham's introduction to international rugby could hardly have been less glamorous.

He made his Wales debut against Georgia at an empty Parc y Scarlets in November 2020, with Covid-19 restrictions keeping supporters away.

His grandfather always believed he would play for Wales, but getting there was one thing. Staying there proved harder.

Part of Wales' Six Nations-winning squad in 2021, Botham subsequently spent more than two and a half years away from the international side.

Injuries and competition played their part. But perhaps his greatest qualities were not always easy to appreciate.

His game was built less on spectacular breaks than on repeated collisions, defensive work and battles at the breakdown.

In that respect, his career echoes another Cardiff flanker, Josh Navidi.

Navidi made his Wales debut in 2013 but waited four years for his second cap.

Long regarded as an outstanding regional player rather than an international star, his strength, work rate and dominance in contact eventually made him indispensable to Wales.

He won 33 caps and toured with the British and Irish Lions.

Botham has followed a similar path. A gifted athlete, his greatest strengths are not always obvious from the stands or on television.

Sam Warburton spotted them years ago.

"I remember seeing him when he first came to Cardiff," said the former Wales and Lions captain.

"His footwork for contact was amazing, just how explosive he was over five, ten metres."

Warburton believes Botham has the attributes of a top international blindside flanker.

"Really strong in contact. Gets great numbers in the gym. He's fast. He's fit. He's probably the best athlete that Wales have in the back row," Warburton added.

One training session with Botham helped convince Warburton his own playing days were numbered.

"I was linked up with James Botham and that's when I realised the flame had gone," he recalled.

"He was full beans going for it and I remember thinking, in the nicest way, I don't care."

For a player whose career was built on an insatiable appetite for physical confrontation, it was telling.

Warburton realised the aggression and hunger that had driven him to the top were gone.

Botham, meanwhile, was just getting started.

Former Wales hooker Scott Baldwin shared a room with Botham on a Barbarians tour, where the social traditions are almost as famous as the rugby.

After a few drinks one evening, Botham decided he still needed a fitness session, so he ran a mile to a nearby pitch, completed his drills and jogged back to rejoin his team-mates.

"He was fully committed to the social, but he had to get his bit in," Baldwin recalled.

Baldwin believes that dedication is evident on the field, even if it often goes unnoticed.

"We'd probably underestimate how much work he gets through every game," he added. "His ability to slow ball down is next level."

And then there is his willingness to chase lost causes: "He's the kid that will chase every kick, whether he's going to get there or not."

Warburton believes Botham has made his case to become Wales' established blindside flanker.

"I think he's definitely stamped down his name at six," he said.

At 28, Botham has taken the long road to becoming an overnight success. With his first child due this week, it promises to be a momentous few days off the field, too.

His surname will always invite comparisons. Any profile of James will inevitably mention his grandfather. This one, after all, has done exactly that.

But there was nothing inherited about the tackles, the exhaustion or the tears at the final whistle.

On Saturday, James Botham was the star of his own story.

articles.title: Andy Burnham urges caution on lifting Saturday 3pm TV blackout in UK
articles.text:
Andy Burnham has urged caution on lifting the Saturday 3pm TV blackout in the UK, saying the health of the football pyramid should come first.

The rule was introduced in the 1960s to encourage fans to attend lower league games and prevents matches from being shown on UK television between 2:45pm and 5:15pm on Saturdays.

The blackout, which is enforced by Article 48 of the Uefa Statutes and is imposed by the English and Scottish football associations, comes into effect when 50% of fixtures in the top two divisions are scheduled to kick off at 3pm.

The Premier League is in the middle of a record £6.7bn domestic TV deal for Sky and TNT to show up to 270 live games a season.

But there could be room for change with the 3pm rule in the upcoming broadcast cycle, as the rights deals for the Premier League, EFL and SPFL all end in 2028-29.

The prime minister said any decision to remove the ban would require careful thought about the consequences.

"I would urge a bit of caution [on the blackout], because it does protect the income of lower-league clubs," Burnham said.

articles.title: United States 6-2 Canada: women’s ice hockey world championship 2026 final – as it happened
articles.text:
Final: USA 6-2 Canada

The United States are world champions again! Hilary Knight and Kelly Pannek score twice each as the Americans complete a historic golden double, adding the world championship to the Olympic title they won in Milan in February.

Canada struck first through Sarah Fillier, but the US roared back with five unanswered goals before cruising to their 12th world title. The Americans finish the tournament unbeaten, having trailed for just five minutes and 14 seconds across seven games, all during tonight’s opening period. A commanding performance from start to finish and a definitive closing statement in this team’s annus mirabilis.

Updated at 15.47 EST

That’s all for today. Thanks as always for following along and be sure to check out the full match report here.

Hayley Scamurra has made a little history of her own. The 31-year-old forward from suburban Buffalo has become the first player to win Olympic gold, world championship gold and the PWHL’s Walter Cup in the same calendar year.

Scamurra won the Walter Cup with the Montreal Victoire in May, added Olympic gold with the United States in Milan in February and completed the treble with Monday’s 6-2 victory over Canada in Herning.

And she put her own finishing touch on the achievement, scoring into an empty net with 3.27 remaining to seal the Americans’ 12th world title.

Caroline Harvey named MVP of the tournament

The US have swept the three individual awards handed out by the tournament directorate, putting another exclamation point on their charmed run to world championship gold.

Caroline Harvey was named the tournament’s most valuable player and best defender, while Aerin Frankel took best goalkeeper honors and captain Hilary Knight was named best forward.

Harvey and Knight also made the media-voted All-Star Team, alongside Canadian forwards Jessie Eldridge and Sarah Fillier, Sweden defender Mira Jungaker and Austria goaltender Selma Luggin.

Luggin’s selection is particularly noteworthy: the Austrian helped her country win its relegation game to retain a place in the top division, earning All-Star recognition despite playing for a team at the opposite end of the standings from the champions.

The Star-Spangled Banner rings out inside Herning Hockey Arena as the American players stand arm in arm, singing along beneath the rafters. Gold medals draped from around their necks, the world champions are basking in the moment after their 6-2 victory over Canada.

Updated at 16.00 EST

Kelly Pannek, who scored twice, credited the Americans’ collective drive for their remarkable run of success, which has now delivered Olympic and world championship gold in the same calendar year.

“I just think it’s the way everyone keeps trying to push each other to get better,” Pannek said afterward. “Everyone trusts that we’re pushing ourselves, and then we come together as a group. It’s just so natural.”

Pannek, who was named the team’s player of the game, pointed to the blend of established stars and emerging talent as a key ingredient.

“You have players that have stayed at the top, like Hilary, and players that have made their way to the top, like Caroline Harvey, and everyone in between. It’s just such a team effort. We play gritty at times, we play skilled at times, and it’s just super fun to be a part of.”

Sarah Fillier, to no one’s surprise, took player of the game honors for Canada after scoring both of her team’s goals.

Updated at 15.45 EST

Final: USA 6-2 Canada

The United States are world champions again! Hilary Knight and Kelly Pannek score twice each as the Americans complete a historic golden double, adding the world championship to the Olympic title they won in Milan in February.

Canada struck first through Sarah Fillier, but the US roared back with five unanswered goals before cruising to their 12th world title. The Americans finish the tournament unbeaten, having trailed for just five minutes and 14 seconds across seven games, all during tonight’s opening period. A commanding performance from start to finish and a definitive closing statement in this team’s annus mirabilis.

Updated at 15.47 EST

GOAL! USA 6-2 Canada (Scamurra 56:33)

USA 6-2 Canada, 3.27, 3rd period

That should settle it! Hayley Scamurra slides the puck into the empty net after Canada pull Desbiens for an extra attacker. Hilary Knight picks up the assist, her third point of the night.

And what a 2026 it’s been for Scamurra, who is now minutes away from completing a remarkable personal treble: Olympic gold, the PWHL’s Walter Cup and world championship gold, all in the same calendar year. The Americans are closing in on a historic double of their own.

USA 5-2 Canada, 4.52, 3rd period

Emma Bowling crashes into Aerin Frankel just before the TV timeout, but the US goaltender is OK after the collision. Canada have pulled Desbiens for an extra attacker as play resumes, throwing everything forward in a desperate attempt to erase the three-goal deficit.

USA 5-2 Canada, 8.17, 3rd period

The Americans are just over eight minutes from historic golden double as the teams pause for a TV timeout.

USA 5-2 Canada, 10.24, 3rd period

Renata Fast returns to the ice after Canada kill off a penalty they could scarcely afford to concede on. The Americans still lead by three, but Canada have survived another dangerous two minutes and kept their flickering hopes alive.

USA 5-2 Canada, 12.24, 3rd period

Renata Fast is sent to the box for boarding, but only after an extended delayed penalty during which the Americans keep possession for nearly a full minute.

USA 5-2 Canada (Fillier 43:28)

USA 5-2 Canada, 16.32, 3rd period

Well, Canada aren’t going quietly. A scant 40 seconds after Eden put the Americans four goals to the good, Sarah Fillier races clear on a breakaway and rifles a gorgeous shot over Aerin Frankel’s shoulder to pull one back.

It’s the second goal of the night for the Georgetown, Ontario, native, with Kristin O’Neill and Renata Fast collecting the assists. Three goals in less than two minutes to start the third period. So much for a quiet finish.

Updated at 15.10 EST

GOAL! USA 5-1 Canada (Eden 42:48)

USA 5-1 Canada, 17.12, 3rd period

The floodgates have opened in Herning! Lacey Eden is left all alone to finish a gorgeous cross-ice pass from Joy Dunne, ripping a shot past Desbiens to give the Americans a four-goal lead.

Caroline Harvey picks up the secondary assist as the US score twice in the opening three minutes of the final period. What was a tense gold-medal encounter has suddenly become a rout and the Americans are closing in on a historic double.

Updated at 15.14 EST

GOAL! USA 4-1 Canada (Pannek 41:29)

USA 4-1 Canada, 18.31, 3rd period

The Americans have struck again! Just 89 seconds into the third period, Kelly Pannek gets her second goal of the night, redirecting Cayla Barnes’ shot from the point past Ann-Renée Desbiens to stretch the US lead to three.

Lee Stecklein picks up the secondary assist on Pannek’s fifth goal of the tournament. After breaking a 1-1 tie midway through the second period, Pannek has now supplied two of the biggest goals of the night. The United States have tacked on a crucial insurance goal early in the final period with the gold medal in sight.

USA 3-1 Canada, 20.00, 3nd period

The puck has dropped for the third period.

The Americans are one period away from completing an unprecedented calendar-year sweep of the two biggest prizes in international women’s hockey. Having won Olympic gold in Milan in February, the Americans can become the first US team to add the world championship in the same year.

And despite the parade of penalties in that frenetic second period, the stat sheet suggests the Americans have earned their two-goal cushion. They’ve outshot Canada 19-13 through 40 minutes, converted one of three power plays and – crucially – killed off all five Canadian advantages.

The US have spent 12 minutes in the penalty box to Canada’s six, yet somehow emerged from the middle frame with a 3-1 lead. Twenty more minutes of that defensive resilience and the John Wroblewski’s side will have made history.

US forward Hayley Scamurra praised her team’s composure during a penalty-filled second period that saw the Americans turn a 1-1 deadlock into a 3-1 lead.

“I was really proud of us, how we handled all that adversity,” Scamurra told TSN during the second intermission. “A few times we were maybe on our heels a little bit with the penalties, but I was really proud of our penalty kill and the way we attacked after those. I think we got a lot of momentum for ourselves.”

The 31-year-old from Williamsville, just outside Buffalo, is also chasing a remarkable personal milestone: completing hockey’s Triple Gold Club in a single year, having already won Olympic gold and the PWHL’s Walter Cup with Montreal.

“It’s just been unbelievable,” she said. “I’m just so honored to be with the teams that I’ve been with. Some amazing players and leaders that I’ve been able to be a part of.”

Asked about protecting the two-goal lead over the final 20 minutes, Scamurra is to the point. “It’s just sticking to our game plan, sticking to what we’re really good at. As long as we keep attacking and playing forward, I think we’re going to do a really great job here.”

Updated at 14.52 EST

End of 2nd period: USA 3-1 Canada

The “U-S-A!” chants are gathering in volume inside Kvik Hockey Arena as the Americans head into the second intermission with a two-goal lead.

Kelly Pannek put the defending champions ahead midway through the period before Hilary Knight struck her second of the night on a four-on-three power play, capping a chaotic sequence of penalties.

Canada have 20 minutes to find a way back into this one, or the Americans will be celebrating their 12th world championship.

Updated at 14.45 EST

GOAL! USA 3-1 Canada (Knight 37:51)

USA 3-1 Canada, 2.09, 2nd period

Hilary Knight strikes again! The American captain hammers home a one-timer on the four-on-three power play to give the United States a two-goal cushion late in the second period.

Megan Keller and Taylor Fox pick up the assists, with Fox’s 13th of the tournament setting a new single-edition world championship record.

It’s Knight’s second goal of the night and ninth of the competition, a personal best at the age of 37. After trailing for the first time all tournament, the defending champions have overturned the deficit with three unanswered goals and are suddenly in command.

Updated at 14.43 EST

USA 2-1 Canada, 2.25, 2nd period

Another penalty! Canada’s Danielle Serdachny is sent off for tripping, just 34 seconds after the Americans were penalized for too many players on the ice.

That makes three penalties in the space of 90 seconds. The US now have a four-on-three advantage in a suddenly chaotic finish to the second period.

USA 2-1 Canada, 2.59, 2nd period

And now the Americans are penalized for having too many players on the ice! Hannah Bilka heads to the box to serve the two-minute bench minor, cutting short the US power play.

We’ll have four-on-four hockey for the next 64 seconds before Canada get a brief advantage of their own.

USA 2-1 Canada, 3.55, 2nd period

Moments after killing off their fourth – and dodgiest – penalty of the night, the Americans get a power play of their own as Canada’s Renata Fast is sent to the box for tripping.

USA 2-1 Canada, 6.06, 2nd period

Well, here’s something you don’t see every day. The United States have been assessed a two-minute bench minor for abuse of officials, with Abbey Murphy sent to the penalty box to serve it.

A rare call at any level, let alone in a world championship final. Canada have a chance to draw level on the power play.

USA 2-1 Canada, 6.57, 2nd period

The teams pause for another TV timeout with the US outshooting Canada 6-4 in the period and 17-12 overall.

GOAL! USA 2-1 Canada (Pannek 31:33)

USA 2-1 Canada, 8.27, 2nd period

The Americans take the lead! Hayley Scamurra delivers a superb cross-crease pass to Kelly Pannek, who hammers home a first-time shot past Ann-Renée Desbiens.

It’s the Minnesota Frost forward’s fourth goal of the tournament, with Scamurra and Grace Zumwinkle credited with the assists.

After trailing for the first time at this world championship, the United States have turned the game around midway through the second period.

Updated at 14.29 EST

USA 1-1 Canada, 9.17, 2nd period

The Canadians kill off the penalty, thanks in no small part to Ann-Renée Desbiens, who produces a spectacular save to deny Abbey Murphy from point-blank range.

USA 1-1 Canada, 11.17, 2nd period

Now the United States will go on the power play for the first time after the Canadian goalscorer Fillier heads to the box for two minutes on a tripping penalty.

USA 1-1 Canada, 12.44, 2nd period

The Americans hold a 12-9 advantage in shots on goal at the first media timeout of the second period.

Updated at 14.18 EST

USA 1-1 Canada, 14.21, 2nd period

And it’s another tidy penalty kill for the United States, who deny the Canadians a single shot on goal during the power play.

The Americans cleared the puck repeatedly as Canada struggled to establish themselves in the attacking zone. Hayley Scamurra even creates a shorthanded chance at the other end, but her effort was turned back.

Updated at 14.16 EST

USA 1-1 Canada, 16.21, 2nd period

Another penalty for the Americans. Megan Keller for high-sticking. Canada’s power play will get a third chance.

USA 1-1 Canada, 19.08, 2nd period

The teams are back to even strength as the American penalty kill remains 100% for the tournament. A smattering of “U-S-A! U-S-A!” chants can be heard in the crowd.

USA 1-1 Canada, 20.00, 2nd period

We’re off and skating in the second period with 52 seconds to go in the Canadian power play.

Canada’s Jessie Eldridge sounded pleased with her team’s opening period after setting up Sarah Fillier’s goal.

“I think I know if I can get Filly the puck, she’s going to put it in the net,” Eldridge told a TSN reporter during the first intermission. “It’s been working so far. We’re hoping to get a couple more.”

Eldridge was part of the Canadian team who won gold in this same building four years ago, but played down the significance of that experience.

“I think we’re a completely different roster here. Both sides, too,” the Montreal Victoire forward said. “We’re just going to keep playing our way.”

And her assessment of the opening 20 minutes? “It’s great hockey. I think it’s going to be a lot of fun in the next 40.”

Updated at 14.08 EST

End 1st period: USA 1-1 Canada

We’re all square after 20 minutes in Herning, with Sarah Fillier’s opener for Canada canceled out by Hilary Knight’s eighth goal of the tournament. The Americans have outshot the Canadians 11-8.

Canada will begin the second period with just under a minute remaining on the power play.

Updated at 14.14 EST

USA 1-1 Canada, 1.08, 1st period

A second penalty on the United States. It’s going to be two minutes for holding on Pannek as Wroblewski throws his arms up in disbelief after having a look at the replay. It’s another chance for Canada’s tournament-best power play, a unit that entered today’s game converting at 43%.

Updated at 13.47 EST

GOAL! USA 1-1 Canada (Knight 16:17)

USA 1-1 Canada, 3.31, 1st period

Hilary Knight pounces on a rebound in front of goal to draw the Americans level, sending chants of “U-S-A!” ringing around the arena in Herning.

Laila Edwards makes a lovely move at the point to create the opening, with Tessa Janecke also picking up an assist as Knight buries the loose puck past Ann-Renée Desbiens.

It’s Knight’s eighth goal and 11th point of the tournament, and the United States are back on level terms with less than four minutes remaining in the opening period.

Updated at 13.56 EST

USA 0-1 Canada, 5.20, 1st period

Canada have the lead through Sarah Fillier – the second coming of Marie-Philip Poulin? – but the Americans are beginning to turn the screw in the attacking zone.

Kelly Pannek tests Desbiens with a sharp-angle effort from close range, only for the Canadian goaltender to turn it away.

The shots are level at 6-6 with just over five minutes remaining in the opening period.

GOAL! USA 0-1 Canada (Fillier 11:03)

USA 0-1 Canada, 9.57, 1st period

Canada strike first! Sarah Fillier redirects the puck past Aerin Frankel with a deft backhand finish to give the Canadians the lead midway through the opening period. Jessie Eldridge and Rosalie Tremblay pick up the assists.

That’s five goals in five games for Fillier, who missed Canada’s first two matches through injury but has scored in every appearance since.

And for the first time at this world championship, the United States find themselves trailing.

Updated at 13.40 EST

USA 0-0 Canada, 9.57, 1st period

The US kill the penalty, limiting Canada to a single shot, and they’re back to even strength with Harvey on the ice.

USA 0-0 Canada, 11.57, 1st period

The first power play of the night goes to Canada as Harvey is given two minutes for interference on Fillier.

USA 0-0 Canada, 13.o7, 1st period

Canada are enjoying more time in the attacking zone as we reach the first media timeout. Jessie Eldridge goes down under pressure in the American zone, while Caroline Harvey loses her stick in the scramble, but there’s no penalty.

Updated at 13.34 EST

USA 0-0 Canada, 16.16, 1st period

Canada have their first good look at goal as Jessie Eldridge carries the puck into the American zone and sends a backhander toward the net. Frankel corrals it comfortably.

At the other end, Laila Edwards unleashes a blistering shot from the point through traffic, but Desbiens tracks the puck all the way and makes the save.

Both goaltenders have been called into action in a lively opening four minutes.

Updated at 13.17 EST

USA 0-0 Canada, 20.00, 1st period

We’re under way from Kvik Hockey Arena in Herning!

Updated at 14.40 EST

The lineups are confirmed for tonight’s gold-medal game, with Aerin Frankel in goal for the United States and Ann-Renée Desbiens between the pipes for Canada.

US captain Hilary Knight starts alongside forwards Tessa Janecke and Alex Carpenter, with Megan Keller and Laila Edwards the starting defensive pair. Frankel enters the final having set American records for career wins and shutouts at the women’s world championship.

Canada captain Laura Stacey starts up front with Caitlin Kraemer and Daryl Watts, while Renata Fast and Nicole Gosling form the starting defensive pair. Desbiens has been similarly impressive throughout the tournament, conceding just one goal in three starts.

Updated at 13.26 EST

Today’s gold-medal game will be the 201st meeting between the US and Canada in women’s international hockey, a rivalry stretching back to the inaugural world championship final in 1990.

Canada hold the historical advantage, with 109 victories to the Americans’ 90, plus one tie across the first 200 encounters. But the US have enjoyed the upper hand recently, winning the 2025 world championship final and February’s Olympic gold-medal game, both in overtime.

There is another historical wrinkle to today’s showdown: the last time the women’s worlds were staged in Herning, in 2022, Canada beat the US 2-1 in the final. Brianne Jenner scored twice in just 83 seconds during the second period to secure Canada’s 12th world title.

Four years later, the Canadians return to the same city chasing their 14th. The Americans, meanwhile, are looking to close the gap with a 12th championship of their own.

A fit and firing Sarah Fillier is a welcome sight for Canadian fans. The 26-year-old forward missed the first two games of this world championship with an upper-body injury. Since returning, the forward has wasted little time making her presence felt.

Fillier has scored in all four games she has played, including Sunday’s semi-final against Sweden, when she broke a scoreless deadlock with a power-play goal midway through the second period. Sarah Wozniewicz and Emma Maltais added further goals as Canada completed a 3-0 victory.

The 2022 Beijing Olympic champion, who plays for the PWHL’s New York Sirens, has emerged as one of Canada’s most important attacking players. Her scoring touch could prove crucial against a US defense that has conceded only twice in six games.

US goaltender Aerin Frankel has been quietly making history of her own at this world championship, for all the attention lavished on Americans’ headline-grabbing attack,

Frankel recorded her eighth career shutout at the women’s worlds with a 17-save performance in Sunday’s 5-0 semi-final victory over Finland, breaking the American record previously held by Nicole Hensley.

The Boston Fleet goaltender also became the United States’ all-time leader in world championship victories earlier in the tournament, taking her career tally to 19.

With the Americans having conceded just two goals in six games on their way to tonight’s final, Frankel will face a considerably sterner examination against Canada as the US pursue a 12th world title.

Sweden win third-place game

Sweden won the third-place game earlier today, beating Finland 2-1 in a shootout to claim their first medal at the tournament in nearly two decades.

Lina Ljungblom, a forward with the PWHL’s Montreal Victoire, forced overtime with a power-play goal six minutes from the end of regulation after Vancouver Goldeneyes forward Michelle Karvinen had put Finland ahead late in the second period. Hilda Svensson, a 20-year-old Ohio State sophomore, assisted on the equalizer before scoring the decisive shootout goal.

Swedish goaltender Ebba Svensson Traff turned back 29 shots through overtime and stopped four of five shootout attempts. Finland’s Sanni Ahola, of the Ottawa Charge, finished with 35 saves.

It is Sweden’s third world championship bronze, following medals in 2005 and 2007.

Updated at 13.54 EST

If Canada are to halt the Americans’ winning streak, Ann-Renée Desbiens may have to be at her very best. The 32-year-old goaltender has been close to unbeatable in Denmark, allowing just one goal in three starts while posting a tournament-leading .981 save percentage.

Sunday’s 13-save shutout against Sweden was her second in succession and the 10th of her world championship career, leaving her three behind compatriot Kim St-Pierre’s all-time record. It was also her 25th victory at the worlds, extending her own Canadian record.

Desbiens arrives on the back of an outstanding professional season with the Montréal Victoire, whom she helped to their first Walter Cup championship after leading the PWHL with 19 wins and a 1.11 goals-against average.

Against an American attack averaging more than eight goals per game, Canada will need every bit of that form.

Hej, Guardian-læsere and welcome to our live coverage of the 2026 IIHF Women’s World Championship final between the US and Canada. The fiercest rivalry in women’s hockey is renewed tonight in Herning, Denmark, with another world title on the line, less than nine months after the Americans broke Canadian hearts in the Olympic final at Milano Cortina.

The neighboring countries that share the world’s longest international border have exercised an extraordinary duopoly over this competition since its inception in 1990, combining to win all 24 previous editions. Canada lead the all-time count with 13 titles to the US’s 11, but the balance of power has shifted south of the border in recent years. The Americans are defending world champions after a dramatic 4-3 overtime victory in last year’s final in the Czech Republic, and followed that with a 2-1 overtime win over Canada for Olympic gold in February, sealed by Megan Keller’s winner.

The US arrive in flying form. John Wroblewski’s team have won 20 consecutive games in international competition since their defeat to Canada in the 2024 world championship final, including six straight victories at this tournament by a combined score of 50-2. Sunday’s 5-0 semi-final demolition of Finland followed an even more emphatic 14-0 quarter-final rout of hosts Denmark. Canada, meanwhile, booked their place with a 3-0 shutout of Sweden, behind goals from Sarah Fillier, Sarah Wozniewicz and Emma Maltais.

There have been individual milestones aplenty for the Americans. Caroline Harvey, the 24-year-old defender, has racked up 15 points in six games, a single-tournament record for a player at her position. Taylor Fox has equaled the tournament record with 12 assists, while captain Hilary Knight, now 37 and the US team’s north star for so many years, continues to extend her extraordinary world championship records: 74 goals and 130 points in 93 appearances. Between the pipes, Aerin Frankel recorded her eighth career shutout at the worlds against Finland, another American record.

Yet for all their dominance against the rest of the field, the Americans know Canada represent an altogether different challenge. These familiar opponents have met in 23 of the previous 24 world championship finals, and their last two major title encounters have required overtime to separate them.

Puck drop is scheduled for 1pm ET (7pm local time), with live television coverage on NHL Network in the United States and TSN and RDS in Canada. Canadian viewers can also stream the game on TSN’s digital platforms. We’ll have all the buildup, team news and live updates from Herning right here.

Bryan will be here shortly to marshal our coverage of the women’s ice hockey world championship final between the United States and Canada. In the meantime, here’s the Associated Press report on Sunday’s semi-final twin bill:

The United States and Canada will renew their rivalry in the final of the women’s ice hockey world championship on Monday.

In the semi-finals on Sunday, defending champions the US blanked Finland 5-0 before Canada shut out Sweden 3-0.

US captain Hilary Knight had a goal and an assist, with Kelly Pannek, Alex Carpenter, Caroline Harvey and Lacey Eden also scoring.

Aerin Rankel stopped 17 shots for her eighth career world championship shutout and 19th victory.

The Americans jumped out to a 2-0 lead in the opening period after Pannek netted the opener from the low slot 6:36 in and Knight fed Carpenter with a backhand pass from behind the net to double the advantage with 3:26 remaining.

Harvey, Eden and Knight extended the lead to 5-0 in the span of 1min 35sec in the second period.

Tournament leading scorer Harvey moved to 15 points from six games. Knight extended her record points tally to 130, with 74 goals and 56 assists in 93 games at the worlds.

Finland pulled goalie Sanni Ahola, who made 20 saves, after the second period, with Emilia Kyrkko taking over and finishing with nine saves.

Sarah Fillier, Sarah Wozniewicz and Emma Maltais scored a goal each and goalie Ann-Renée Desbiens made 13 saves for Canada’s shutout.

Fillier skated to the left circle before breaking the deadlock with a snap shot high into the net 7:15 into the middle period.

The forward extended her goal streak to four games. She missed the first two games of the tournament with an upper-body injury.

Wozniewicz made it 2-0 on a breakaway and Maltais added the third in the final period.

Finland will face Sweden in the bronze-medal game after finishing third last year.

Canada have won 13 world titles, followed by the US with 11.

The Americans won the 2025 title in the Czech Republic and Olympic gold at the Milan-Cortina Games in February, beating Canada in overtime in both finals.

Hilary Knight and Kelly Pannek score twice each as the Americans complete a historic golden double, adding the world championship to the Olympic title they won in Milan in February. articles.title: Trump backs return of ex-Nvidia boss after 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign launched
articles.text:
US President Donald Trump has said he "would certainly not mind" seeing Jensen Huang handed back his job as allies of the former Nvidia chief executive called for him to be reinstated.

Huang resigned as boss of the AI chip giant last week after the emergence of two affairs, one of which was with a woman suspected of spying for China and another allegedly with one of his employees.

It created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms, which is a key part of the AI rollout, but the BBC has been told Nvidia's board is not considering reinstating Huang.

Meanwhile the Trump administration on Monday said it will further restrict China's ​access to AI chips from companies like Nvidia.

Fellow tech bosses, including SpaceX's Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, have backed a campaign to get Nvidia's board to "Bring Jensen Back".

The pair were among more than 175,000 signatories of an open letter calling for the board to reinstate Huang while an ongoing internal probe is conducted.

President Trump gave his views on Huang's future on Monday, saying he "would certainly not mind" seeing the former boss given his job back.

"I guess maybe one lesson is more important than another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that," he told reporters as he left the White House.

The Trump administration on Monday also issued new restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres, which allow Chinese companies to access advanced AI chips to train AI models.

The move came ahead of Trump's meeting with Chinese President Xi Jingping.

The new rules will require companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for US export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to cut down on them being illegally diverted to China.

The president's comments on Huang came after the "Stand with Jensen" campaign group, which claims to be made up of current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters, demanded the return of the former chief executive.

They expressed concerns the ex-Nvidia boss "was removed without meaningful due process".

Huang had been expected to weather the storm following the revelation of an affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy.

However, he resigned last Thursday after a second extra-marital relationship emerged, allegedly with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him.

The scandal-hit tech boss is now discussing a possible return to Nvidia with confidants, according to the Financial Times, external, though the publication reported Nvidia's board is not considering reappointing him.

A person familiar with the thinking of Nvidia's board told the BBC its directors are not interested in bringing Huang back to lead the company.

A representative for Huang declined to comment on the report.

The so-called war room also wants to get support for Huang from the White House.

President Trump has spoken in glowing terms about Huang since the scandal broke out, and also said he believed Huang when the former Nvidia boss told him he had "no idea she was a spy".

Trump's view is at odds with his Treasury Secretary, Scott Bessent, who has called for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company.

The scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end Nvidia chips to Alice Huang's former firm, Megaspeed. China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy.

It has raised questions about the possibility that the chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
